items.prompt: A region’s manufacturing jobs rise 200 to 240 while total jobs rise 1,000 to 1,500. Separately, a camp loses work in a predictable quiet season and technical vacancies remain unfilled because applicants lack required training. (a) Describe three relevant features (6). items.canonical_answer: (a) Manufacturing count rises 40. Its share falls 20 to 16 percent. The camp has a recurring seasonal gap while technical jobs show a skill mismatch. (b) Count and share differ because overall jobs grow faster. The quiet-season cause is seasonal, not proof of a general downturn. Vacancies and missing skills support structural mismatch, not an inference of unwillingness. The data do not establish all residents’ labour-force status. (c) Investigate feasible off-season demand for camp workers and relevant accessible training for actual technical opportunities. Check transport, costs and completion rather than promise jobs. The judgement should address each evidenced barrier and monitor employment outcomes, not use one general measure for all cases.
marking_guidance: Context: region. Parts/allocation: (a) count, share, causes 2 each=6. (b) ratio mechanism 2, seasonal distinction 2, mismatch 2, data limit 1=7. (c) matched remedies 3, feasibility checks 2, conditional judgement 2=7. Mechanism: status or demand changes must be traced; judgement uses actual job outcomes.

items.prompt: A labour dataset defines 600 employed and 150 unemployed in a working-age population 1,000. Twenty unemployed people later stop seeking, with no one entering work. Policymakers propose judging success solely from the unemployment rate. (a) Define labour force participation (2). (b) Explain the original participation and unemployment rates (4). (c) Explain the effect of the later status change (7). (d) Discuss whether the proposed success judgement is justified (7).
items.canonical_answer: (a) Involvement in employed-plus-unemployed labour force. (b) Labour force 750; participation 75 percent. Unemployment 150/750 ×100 =20 percent. (c) Employment stays 600; unemployed become 130 and labour force 730. Participation falls to 73 percent, while unemployment rate 130/730 is about 17.81 percent. The lower unemployment rate comes from exit, not job creation. Reasons for exit are not supplied. (d) The rate usefully describes one labour-force measure, but does not show improved access to work here. Employment, participation, status flows and causes should also be examined. The supported judgement is that no employment success has been demonstrated by the drop alone; assess actual suitable work and the reasons for movement.
marking_guidance: Context: dataset. Parts/allocation: (a) involvement 1, employed/unemployed group 1. (b) correct denominator and rate 2 each=4. (c) counts 2, rates 3, exit mechanism 2=7. (d) measure usefulness 2, employment/participation limits 2, evidence-based judgement 3=7. Mechanism: status or demand changes must be traced; judgement uses actual job outcomes.

items.prompt: Evaluate whether an authority should apply a single retraining programme to all joblessness when evidence includes weak demand, seasonal gaps and job-search delays as well as skills shortages (9).

Against: it does not itself create missing customers, remove recurring off-season demand or solve every information delay. It costs time/resources and participation does not assure an offer. Judgement: diagnose and target the barriers, combining appropriate measures where evidence supports them. The condition for retraining’s success is relevant accessible learning linked to real opportunities and other access needs. One programme is not justified by the unemployment label alone.

items.prompt: The Fold Pack firm has two complete monthly plans. Manual production yields revenue N$28,000 and total cost N$22,000. A machine plan yields N$34,000 revenue and N$29,000 total cost, including all relevant training and maintenance for this illustration. It reduces sealing tasks but requires an operator. (a) Describe three relevant features (6). (b) Examine the implications for the profit goal and factor demand (7). (c) Suggest a decision using these data and their limits (7).
items.canonical_answer: (a) Manual profit is N$6,000. Machine profit is N$5,000 despite higher revenue. The machine substitutes for some tasks while requiring operator labour. (b) The higher-revenue machine plan gives N$1,000 less profit because its additional cost exceeds the receipt increase. Factor requirements change in composition, not simply from labour to no labour. The complete stated plans support the comparison for this month, but do not establish later demand or quality benefits. (c) If this month’s profit is the goal, choose the manual plan from these alternatives. Investigate future consistency, orders and complete costs before changing for a longer period. A machine could be justified if later gains exceed relevant costs, but those gains are not shown. The judgement should retain the stated period and avoid treating higher output or revenue as sufficient evidence.
marking_guidance: Context: Fold Pack. Parts/allocation: (a) two profit figures and task change, developed 2 each = 6. (b) profit mechanism 3, substitution/complementarity 2, time limit 2 = 7. (c) current decision 2, relevant future evidence 3, conditional judgement 2 = 7.

items.canonical_answer: (a) Demand for a productive input derived from demand for its output. (b) Order volume affects useful equipment utilisation. Technical suitability for varied designs affects productive contribution and setup needs. Training uses time and workers may face adjustment; net employment cannot be inferred without the new requirements and output response. Seek a complete comparison and realistic volume evidence before deciding; the purchase price alone is insufficient.

items.prompt: Explain what demand elasticity magnitude 2 means when based on a 20 percent quantity fall following a 10 percent price rise.

marking_guidance: Relationship: twice proportionate response 1; evidence: 20/10 1; explanation: elastic and ratio rather than percentage 2.

items.prompt: A shop sells 100 packets a week of maize meal and 100 packets a week of one brand of crisps, each at N$20 a packet. Both prices rise to N$30. Weekly sales of maize meal fall to 75 packets and sales of the crisps fall to 25 packets. Assume straight demand lines and unchanged other demand conditions. Use these data to draw both demand curves on the same axes, with price on the vertical axis. Show the change for each product and label each curve with its price elasticity of demand (PED), calculated from the initial values (4).
items.canonical_answer: Draw both demand curves through the original point R (100, N$20) on the same labelled axes: price (N$ per packet) vertically, quantity demanded (packets per week) horizontally. The maize meal curve also passes through (75, N$30) and the crisps curve through (25, N$30); an arrow along each curve shows the movement from R as price rises. Price rises by 50 per cent. Maize meal: −25% ÷ 50% = −0.5, so demand is inelastic (magnitude below 1). Crisps: −75% ÷ 50% = −1.5, so demand is elastic (magnitude above 1). Because both curves share the same axes and starting point, the flatter crisps curve is the more elastic one over this change.
marking_guidance: Diagram: both demand curves drawn through the original point (100 packets, N$20) on common labelled axes, with price vertical (1).
Change: movement along each curve from that point to (75, N$30) for maize meal and to (25, N$30) for crisps (1).
Labels: maize meal PED = −25% ÷ 50% = −0.5, inelastic (1).
Labels: crisps PED = −75% ÷ 50% = −1.5, elastic (1).

items.canonical_answer: Draw both supply curves through the original point R (50, N$400) on the same labelled axes: price (N$ per chair) vertically, quantity supplied (chairs per month) horizontally. Workshop B: +20% ÷ 50% = 0.4, so supply is inelastic (below 1): near capacity it can add little output in the short term. items.prompt: The Reed Baskets stall raises price from N$40 to N$44. Weekly quantity demanded falls from 150 to 144. Other demand conditions are unchanged; use initial values. Costs are not supplied. Nearby sellers offer similar baskets. (a) Describe three features of the price and quantity data (6). (b) Examine the implications for responsiveness and revenue (7). (c) Suggest how the owner should use the result in deciding future prices (7).
items.canonical_answer: (a) Price rises N$4, which is 10 percent. Quantity falls six baskets, which is 4 percent. Price and quantity demanded move in opposite directions, with a proportionately smaller quantity response. (b) Demand elasticity magnitude is 4/10=0.4, inelastic for this change. Revenue rises from N$6,000 to N$6,336, an increase of N$336. The quantity loss is proportionately smaller than the price gain. This is revenue, not profit, because costs are absent. (c) Use the observed inelastic response as evidence for this particular change, but do not assume further rises behave identically. Similar sellers offer alternatives and buyers may switch after more time. Compare costs and longer-term quantity response before judging profitability. A cautious pricing review is defensible if it checks whether the observed response persists and whether the additional receipts exceed any relevant cost changes.
marking_guidance: Context: Reed Baskets. Parts/allocation: (a) price pattern 2, quantity pattern 2, proportionate comparison 2 = 6. (b) coefficient/classification 2, revenue evidence 2, inelastic mechanism 2, profit boundary 1 = 7. (c) relevant evidence 2, substitutes/time 2, conditional judgement including costs 3 = 7.

items.prompt: (a) Define price elasticity of demand (2). (b) Define price elasticity of supply (2). (c) Explain why a coefficient is not a percentage (2). (d) Explain the difference between inelastic and perfectly inelastic demand (2). (e) Explain one reason close substitutes can affect demand responsiveness (2). (f) Explain why available adjustment time can affect supply responsiveness (2). (g) Explain why total revenue is not profit (2). (h) Explain why a signed demand coefficient of minus two can be classified elastic (2).
items.canonical_answer: (a) Percentage demand-quantity response divided by percentage price change. (b) Percentage supply-quantity response divided by percentage price change. (c) It is a ratio of two percentage changes, leaving no percentage unit. (d) Inelastic can have a small non-zero response; perfectly inelastic has none. (e) Alternatives let buyers switch when price rises, increasing potential response. (f) More time may allow producers to adjust capacity or output. (g) Revenue is sales receipts, while profit requires costs to be deducted. (h) Classification uses magnitude two, which exceeds one, rather than treating the negative sign as low responsiveness.
marking_guidance: Parts/allocation and precision: eight at 2 each. (a/b) correct quantity side + price ratio; (c) ratio + no percent unit; (d) small response + zero boundary; (e) substitutes + switching mechanism; (f) time + capacity adjustment; (g) receipts + cost deduction; (h) magnitude + above-one classification.

items.prompt: The Frame Craft workshop raises price from N$80 to N$88. Weekly quantity demanded falls from 200 to 160 with other demand conditions unchanged. The workshop could offer more output because it has spare capacity, but buyers have several alternative suppliers. Use initial values. No cost figures are supplied. (a) Define total revenue (2). (b) Explain two reasons why demand and supply responsiveness could differ here (4). (c) Explain the price change’s effect on demand responsiveness and revenue using the data (7). (d) Discuss whether spare capacity alone justifies a further price rise (7).
items.canonical_answer: (a) Sales receipts, price multiplied by quantity sold before cost deduction. (b) Buyer alternatives support switching and greater demand responsiveness. Spare workshop capacity supports the producer’s ability to alter output, a supply-side response. (c) Price rises 10 percent; quantity falls 20 percent. Demand elasticity magnitude is two, elastic. Revenue falls from N$16,000 to N$14,080, a reduction of N$1,920. The proportionately larger quantity loss outweighs the price increase. Spare capacity does not change that observed buyer response. (d) Capacity can help meet additional orders, but does not establish that buyers will place them at a higher price. The observed elastic response and alternatives caution against assuming extra revenue. Another price rise needs evidence about the relevant demand response and costs; unused equipment alone is insufficient. The decision should prioritise buyer response and the objective sought, without claiming revenue equals profit. Inelastic demand for a proposed change could support a higher-revenue argument, but the observed response here is elastic and supports the opposite warning.
marking_guidance: Context: Frame Craft. Parts/allocation: (a) sales receipts 1, price-times-quantity before costs 1. (b) demand substitute mechanism 2, supply capacity mechanism 2 = 4. (c) percentage evidence 2, coefficient/classification 2, revenue amounts and causal interpretation 3 = 7. (d) capacity benefit 2, demand-side limitation 2, supported judgement distinguishing revenue/profit and sides 3 = 7.

items.prompt: Evaluate whether a refill station should infer that a price rise will improve its financial performance solely because demand was inelastic in one short trial; costs and longer-term responses are unknown (9).
items.canonical_answer: For: inelastic demand in the relevant trial means the quantity loss was proportionately smaller than the price rise, increasing total revenue for that change. This provides useful evidence about short-run buyer behaviour. Against: buyers may find substitutes over time, and a larger price change may have a different response. Revenue does not measure profit without costs. A one-period result also does not establish the effect on all customers or future sales. Judgement: use the trial as limited evidence and compare repeat demand responses and costs before inferring improved financial performance. The condition is that relevant demand remains inelastic for the proposed change and the resulting receipts relative to costs support the objective. A coefficient alone is insufficient.
marking_guidance: Argument for: inelastic condition and revenue mechanism, up to 4. Argument against: time/size limitations and profit distinction, up to 4. Judgement: distinct condition on relevant response and costs, 1. Total 9.

items.prompt: The Clay Corner workshop advertises a new pottery class. Its poster gives the location and fee; a digital notice shows completed pots and invites bookings. Many intended customers pass the workshop, but some have unreliable internet. No booking results are yet available. (a) Describe three advertising features in this case (6). (b) Examine how the two methods could affect customers' decisions (7). (c) Suggest a suitable communication approach (7).
items.canonical_answer: (a) The poster informs through location and fee. The digital notice uses images to encourage interest. Both carry a booking invitation or information to support action. (b) Passing residents can see local details without internet. Images can help potential customers judge what the class offers, but do not establish that they will book. Customers with unreliable access may miss the digital message. Clear fee and location information can reduce uncertainty, while missing booking details could interrupt action. (c) Keep a clear local poster and use the digital notice as a complement, with consistent fee, timing and contact details. The combination fits passers-by and people who can browse remotely. Check enquiries and bookings against the intended audience before expanding spending. No current evidence proves either method produces more sales.
marking_guidance: Context: Clay Corner. Parts/allocation: (a) three message features with purpose development, 2 each = 6. (b) local information mechanism 2, visual persuasion 2, access/action limits 3 = 7. (c) combination 2, audience justification 3, evidence-based judgement 2 = 7.

items.prompt: The Quiet Desk furniture maker wants customers to know its location and appreciate the finish of its desks. A radio announcement reaches local listeners; a printed leaflet can show photographs and dimensions. The business can afford one initial campaign. No reliable cost-per-customer or response figures are supplied. (a) Define an advertising method (2). (b) Explain two purposes relevant to the campaign (4). (c) Explain how the methods differ in meeting the stated communication needs (7). (d) Discuss which should be tried first (7).
items.canonical_answer: (a) Channel used to communicate advertising to an audience. (b) Inform customers of the location so they can visit. Persuade through the finish so they consider choosing the desks. (c) Radio can announce location and repeat it for local listeners, but cannot show the finish. A leaflet can display photographs and dimensions for later reference, but must reach relevant readers and images may not fully represent the object. Neither establishes actual purchase. (d) A targeted leaflet is defensible if showing finish and dimensions is central and distribution can reach potential customers. Radio may be better where listening reach is strong and finding the location is the main barrier. Given the absent response data, do not claim one has lower cost per customer. Try a method suited to the priority, monitor enquiries and consider the other if the information gap remains.

items.prompt: A farming district fully and efficiently uses its fixed land, labour and equipment to produce maize and cattle. Its yearly production schedule is A (0 t maize, 80 cattle), B (50 t, 75), C (100 t, 60), D (150 t, 35) and E (200 t, 0). Use the schedule to draw the district's production possibility curve (PPC), with maize on the horizontal axis. Plot J (50 t, 40 cattle) and K (100 t, 80 cattle) and state what each shows. Show the change from C to D and state its opportunity cost (4).
items.canonical_answer: Plot A (0, 80), B (50, 75), C (100, 60), D (150, 35) and E (200, 0), with maize (tonnes per year) on the horizontal axis and cattle (head per year) on the vertical axis, and join them with a smooth curve bowed outwards: this is the PPC. J (50, 40) lies inside the curve: resources are unemployed or used inefficiently, because 50 t of maize could be produced alongside 75 cattle. K (100, 80) lies outside the curve: it cannot be reached with the district's present resources and technology. Moving from C to D gives 50 t more maize (an arrow across from C) and 25 fewer cattle (an arrow down to D), so the opportunity cost of the extra 50 t of maize is 25 cattle. From B to C the same 50 t cost only 15 cattle; the cost rises because land and workers better suited to cattle are moved into maize.
marking_guidance: Diagram: original schedule points A to E plotted on labelled axes and joined as one curve bowed outwards (1).
Labels: J inside the curve, identified as unemployed or inefficiently used resources (1).
Labels: K outside the curve, identified as unattainable with present resources and technology (1).
Change: movement from C to D shown as 50 t more maize and 25 fewer cattle, with the opportunity cost of the extra 50 t of maize stated as 25 cattle (1).

context.situation: A farming district choosing between maize and cattle production

items.prompt: A community radio team has one editing computer, one editor and a four-hour evening slot. It can edit either a local-history programme valued by the committee at 18 service points or a road-safety programme valued at 14 comparable service points. A free editing course uses the same evening; its benefits would arrive later and are uncertain. The committee cannot combine the activities tonight. (a) Describe three constraints and their consequences (6). (b) Examine whether the course should be chosen when the committee prioritises future programme quality (7). (c) Suggest a choice if tonight's priority is the largest stated service benefit, identifying the opportunity cost and assumptions (7).
items.canonical_answer: (a) Computer access restricts the editing work; one editor cannot perform the competing activities concurrently; the four-hour slot limits what can be completed tonight. (b) The course could improve editing skill, reduce later mistakes and improve later service. Against this, it sacrifices the best available programme tonight, postpones current service and may not improve relevant skills. Choose it if its relevance and expected future gains justify that sacrifice under the longer-term priority. (c) Edit the local-history programme: 18 exceeds 14. The opportunity cost is the road-safety programme's 14 points, not 32 points. The advantage is 18 − 14 = 4 points. This assumes the activities are feasible and the service valuations are comparable; a new priority or evidence about the course can change the recommendation.

items.prompt: A residents' association can use N$24,000 and its available volunteers either to install shade shelters at a meeting area or to repair a footpath. It cannot complete both this year. (a) Define opportunity cost (2). (b) Explain how funding and volunteer time create constraints (4). (c) Explain what is sacrificed by selecting the shelters and why that sacrifice is not adequately described by the shelters' cash cost alone (7). (d) Discuss whether the association should choose the shelters (7).

(b) The budget supports one project, not the combination; volunteer hours committed to one project cannot perform the competing work in that period. (c) The selected shelters provide a meeting-area benefit. The next-best footpath repair is rejected. Residents lose the improvement in access that repair could deliver. This is a valuable service even without a sale. Spending N$24,000 names a payment, not that forgone service. The comparison concerns this year's constrained choice, assuming the projects are feasible; later resources may allow another decision. (d) Shelters can improve comfort and the usefulness of an already popular space. Footpath repair addresses reported access difficulties and may particularly help older residents. Choose according to the severity, timing and available substitutes for these needs. Prioritise the footpath if the damage is a serious barrier and shelter alternatives exist; prioritise shelters if path access is manageable and summer use is urgent.

items.prompt: Evaluate a decision to use a mobile library's available Saturday trip for a remote village rather than a closer settlement. The opportunity cost is the benefit of the closer trip forgone, not its distance alone. The repair market has a sole supplier protected by costly entry, but demand is still responsive. (d) Funding maintenance could improve reliability and reduce interruption for customers. items.prompt: At a vegetable market, bad weather reduces quantities growers can supply at each price. Buyers’ incomes and preferences are unchanged. Initially price was N$12 per bundle and equilibrium quantity 200 bundles weekly. No new schedule or size of the supply reduction is supplied. (a) Define supply (2). (b) Explain two distinctions needed to analyse the event (4). (c) Explain the effect on the market using a labelled demand-and-supply diagram (7). (d) Discuss whether a trader can conclude that total weekly sales receipts must rise (7).
items.canonical_answer: (a) Quantities producers are willing and able to offer at different prices over a period, other conditions unchanged. (b) Weather changes quantities at given prices, shifting supply rather than causing an own-price movement. Buyers’ conditions are unchanged, so demand stays in place even though quantity demanded changes with price. (c) Draw downward D and upward S0, label E0 and initial price N$12/quantity 200. Shift S left to S1. At the old price demand exceeds the reduced offer, tending to raise price. E1 has higher price and lower quantity; label projections but do not invent figures. (d) Each bundle sells at a higher price, tending to raise receipts per unit, but fewer bundles are sold, tending to reduce receipts. Without the size of each change, total price-times-quantity receipts cannot be established. A trader also needs its own quantity rather than treating the market as its business. The defensible judgement is that total receipts are uncertain, even though the direction of market price is clear.
marking_guidance: Context: vegetable market. Parts/allocation: (a) producer willingness/ability 1, price/period qualifier 1. (b) two distinctions, each contrast + reason 2 = 4. (c) diagram labels/original 2, leftward change 1, shortage mechanism 2, new P/Q directions 2 = 7. (d) higher-price influence 2, lower-quantity influence 2, judgement avoiding unsupported magnitude and market/firm inference 3 = 7.

items.prompt: Evaluate whether a higher observed price is enough evidence for a local food supplier to conclude demand has increased, when no information on quantities or production conditions is supplied (9).
items.canonical_answer: For: higher demand with unchanged supply would raise equilibrium price, so the observation is consistent with a demand increase. Against: a supply reduction with unchanged demand would also raise price but reduce quantity. Both sides may change, and relative shifts matter. A price observation alone cannot identify which determinant moved or establish the quantity effect. Judgement: obtain evidence about quantities, buyer circumstances and producer costs before assigning the cause. The condition for the simple demand explanation is credible evidence that supply conditions were unchanged and buyers wanted more at given prices. The higher price alone does not meet that condition.
marking_guidance: Argument for: demand-shift mechanism with unchanged supply, up to 4. Argument against: alternative supply mechanism and simultaneous changes, up to 4. Judgement: distinct evidence condition, 1. Total 9.

items.prompt: In a coastal town, guest houses want 250, 200, 150, 100 and 50 housekeepers at wages of N$15, 20, 25, 30 and 35 an hour (D1), and 50, 100, 150, 200 and 250 people are willing to work at those wages (S), as in the diagram. More tourists visit the town, and guest houses now want 100 more housekeepers at every wage. Use the diagram to show the original and new equilibrium wage and employment, and explain which curve shifts (4).
items.canonical_answer: The original equilibrium E1 is where D1 crosses S: N$25 an hour and 150 housekeepers. More tourists increase the demand for guest-house rooms, and labour demand is derived from that demand, so labour demand shifts right by 100 at every wage, from D1 to D2 (350, 300, 250, 200 and 150 housekeepers at N$15 to N$35). Labour supply does not shift, because nothing has changed the number of people willing to work at each wage. The new equilibrium E2, where D2 crosses S, is N$30 an hour and 200 housekeepers. The wage rises by N$5 an hour and employment by 50, less than the shift of 100, because the higher wage reduces the number guest houses want and draws more people into the work.
marking_guidance: Diagram: original equilibrium E1 labelled where D1 meets S, at N$25 an hour and 150 housekeepers (1).
Change: labour demand shifted right by 100 at every wage to D2, with the supply curve not moved (1).
Labels: new equilibrium E2 at N$30 an hour and 200 housekeepers (1).
Change: explanation that labour demand is derived from the demand for guest-house rooms, so more tourists raise the demand for housekeepers (1).

The gap may reflect composition and experience as well as skill, so the data do not isolate a single cause or show every technician earns more than every packer. The technician’s nominal pay later rises to N$10,500 while the price index rises from 100 to 105. (a) Define transfer earnings (2). (b) Explain the original reward split (4). (c) Explain how the training and price changes affect the earnings analysis (7). (d) Discuss whether higher nominal pay alone proves the technician is better off (7).
items.canonical_answer: (a) Minimum reward needed to retain a factor in current use. (b) N$8,000 is the retention minimum; N$2,000 is economic rent, the excess above it. Together they equal N$10,000. (c) More qualified applicants can expand labour supply, easing scarcity-related wage pressure if demand is unchanged. Exact real later pay is N$10,500 divided by 105 times 100 = N$10,000 at base prices, so purchasing power is unchanged in this comparison. The new retention minimum is not supplied, so the later rent split cannot be calculated. (d) Higher money earnings may help meet nominal obligations, but matched price growth means no measured purchasing-power gain. Deductions, hours and non-wage conditions could also change and are absent. The supported judgement is that nominal growth alone is insufficient: assess real resources and relevant conditions without inventing changes or assuming the original retention threshold persists.
marking_guidance: Context: technician. Parts/allocation: (a) minimum 1, current-use qualifier 1. (b) minimum identified/explained 2, excess identified/explained 2 = 4. Current saving does not establish that future resources will remain sufficient. (d) Immediate repair is a benefit if the need is urgent. However, checking can become a bottleneck, absence may disrupt the process and repetition may affect motivation. Higher normal output is useful evidence but does not settle resilience or working conditions. (c) Train a backup checker, monitor defects and delays, consult staff about repetition and consider rotation where it improves flexibility. Compare training time/cost with the interruption avoided. items.prompt: The Fresh Pack team produces 480 satisfactory packs in 120 labour hours. After training and a tool-layout change, it produces 540 packs in the same hours with unchanged quality. Its new electronic stock record has occasional downtime. No total cost data is supplied. (a) Describe three relevant features (6). (b) Examine what can be concluded about productivity and its causes (7). (c) Suggest how the firm should evaluate further improvement (7).
items.canonical_answer: (a) Output rises by 60 packs. Labour hours remain 120. Quality is unchanged, while the electronic system is not fully reliable. (b) Output per labour hour rises from four to 4.5, a 12.5 percent increase. Training and reduced tool searching can help explain the process, but both changed together so the exact contribution of each is not isolated. Downtime can offset information benefits. No equal percentage cost or profit gain is established. (c) Track satisfactory output and hours consistently, note errors and downtime, and compare suitable periods after staff learn the system. items.prompt: (a) Define productivity (2). (b) Define labour productivity per hour (2). (c) Explain why more production need not mean more productivity (2). items.prompt: The North Repairs firm adopts an electronic job record while providing staff training. Some workers also need scheduled time for healthcare appointments. items.canonical_answer: (a) Electronic systems processing, storing or communicating information. (b) Shared information can reduce repeated entry and errors. Poor implementation or downtime can instead consume time and delay jobs. (c) Training helps staff use records correctly, while reliability prevents system interruptions. Healthcare access and sensible cover can support continuity and retention of skills. Actual effects depend on needs and implementation; an appointment or health status alone does not establish low work capacity. These processes can reduce avoidable disruption but require an actual output/input comparison. (d) Jobs completed measure production, not productivity alone. Hours and quality may differ, so higher count can coexist with lower satisfactory jobs per hour. Record comparable quality-adjusted output and labour input over an appropriate period, alongside relevant process information. The proposed measure is useful as one output record but inadequate for the productivity conclusion.

items.prompt: An authority considers a temporary import tariff to support local producers. Domestic buyers and firms using the imported input oppose higher costs. Supporters claim future jobs will justify any present expense, but no viability timetable or cost estimates are supplied. (a) Define a tariff (2). (b) Explain two groups’ conflicting interests (4). (c) Explain the possible short- and long-term effects (7). (d) Discuss whether the supporters’ claim is sufficient (7).
items.canonical_answer: (a) Tax on imports. (b) Protected producers may gain demand or time to develop. Buyers and input-using firms may pay more or face less choice. (c) Current support can preserve selected activity while higher input costs affect other production. Longer-term benefits depend on improved viability, not merely the temporary label. Weak rivalry, ongoing dependence or responses abroad can add costs. The distribution of jobs and gains is not uniform. (d) Possible development is a relevant case for support, but the claim that future jobs justify any present cost is unsupported. Seek credible viability evidence, duration, costs and alternatives. Support is justified only if the expected wider gains and feasible conditions warrant the burdens; current information does not establish that.

items.prompt: A town has a privately operated water-delivery service. One operator owns its vehicles and households buy deliveries. A remote area has strong need but few households can afford the proposed fee. The town is considering funding specified deliveries while leaving operation private. (a) Describe three features of the current allocation arrangement (6). (b) Examine whether leaving allocation entirely to the current market could meet the town's access goal (7). (c) Suggest an arrangement to improve access, considering its conditions (7).
items.canonical_answer: (a) Private ownership puts the vehicles under the operator's control; buyers' payments influence where service is financially attractive; decisions respond to expected receipts and costs rather than a public delivery target. (b) The operator can use local knowledge and control costs, but need without paying demand may not fund remote deliveries. Limited competition can further weaken pressure to serve users well. A judgement favouring the current market therefore needs evidence that affordable service is viable; the stated incomes make this uncertain. (c) A mixed arrangement could fund a clear delivery obligation and keep private operation. Specify the area, affordability and performance required, assess the public cost, monitor delivery and compare alternative operators where feasible. Public support is more defensible if access gains justify the resources and monitoring is effective.
marking_guidance: Context/parts/allocation: (a) three current features with their allocation implications, 2 each = 6. (b) mechanism and judgement: market incentives/local knowledge up to 3, low purchasing power/competition/access problems up to 3, supported access judgement 1 = 7. items.prompt: A juice bottler compares factories, each built for one monthly output. Outputs of 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 and 60 thousand litres a month have total costs of N$85,000, N$120,000, N$135,000, N$160,000, N$225,000 and N$360,000. Use these data to calculate average cost and draw the long-run average cost (LRAC) curve. Label where there are economies of scale, the optimum scale and where there are diseconomies of scale, and compare the change in total cost and average cost from 20,000 to 40,000 litres (4).
items.canonical_answer: Average cost = total cost ÷ output: N$8.50, N$6.00, N$4.50, N$4.00, N$4.50 and N$6.00 a litre. Plot these against output (thousand litres a month) and join them as a U-shaped LRAC curve, with average cost (N$ per litre) on the vertical axis. Average cost falls up to 40,000 litres: economies of scale. The lowest point, N$4.00 a litre at 40,000 litres, is the optimum scale. Beyond it average cost rises: diseconomies of scale. From 20,000 to 40,000 litres total cost rises from N$120,000 to N$160,000, but average cost falls from N$6.00 to N$4.00, so it is the fall in cost per litre, not total cost, that shows economies of scale. Each point is a different factory size, so this is a long-run curve, not extra output from one factory.
marking_guidance: Diagram: average cost calculated from the original data as total cost ÷ output (N$8.50, 6.00, 4.50, 4.00, 4.50, 6.00 a litre) and plotted against output as a U-shaped LRAC curve (1).
Labels: economies of scale where LRAC falls, up to 40,000 litres (1).
Labels: optimum scale at the lowest point (40,000 litres, N$4.00 a litre) and diseconomies of scale where LRAC rises beyond it (1).
Change: from 20,000 to 40,000 litres total cost rises from N$120,000 to N$160,000 while average cost falls from N$6.00 to N$4.00 (1).

items.prompt: The Carton Coast considers larger-scale production. A small plan has complete long-run cost N$30,000 for 5,000 satisfactory units; a large plan N$50,000 for 10,000. (b) Bulk terms and specialisation may lower unit resources; coordination difficulties could offset savings through delays or waste. The stated plans show lower average cost but do not isolate each cause. Lower production cost does not prove profit if output is unsold. (c) Verify demand and whether the complete cost assumptions include the extra organisational needs. Pilot or stage growth if the risks cannot be resolved immediately. items.prompt: The Coast Canvas firm sells bags abroad for a fixed 100 foreign units each and imports cloth for a fixed 40 foreign units per bag. The rate moves from N$14 to N$17 per foreign unit. Quantities and foreign prices are unchanged; ignore other costs and charges. The firm receives payments through a commercial bank. (a) Describe three relevant monetary or financial features of the case (6). (b) Examine the effects of the rate change on its receipts and import payments (7). (c) Suggest how the firm should assess whether the change makes expansion worthwhile (7).
items.canonical_answer: (a) Foreign prices require currency conversion. The bank provides a means of receiving customer payments. The change means more N$ per foreign unit, showing a weaker N$ against that currency. (b) Receipts per bag rise from N$1,400 to N$1,700. Cloth costs rise from N$560 to N$680. Receipts less the stated cloth payment rise from N$840 to N$1,020, but this is not profit because other costs are excluded. Fixed foreign prices do not show any price reduction for foreign customers or any demand response. (c) Assess all costs and repayment obligations before expanding, including the higher N$ cost of any imported equipment. Check whether additional customers and production capacity exist and whether a less favourable future rate would remain affordable. The receipt gain on existing bags alone is insufficient evidence for profitable expansion. A modest expansion is more defensible if complete costs, capacity and demand support it; otherwise retain flexibility.
marking_guidance: Context: Coast Canvas. Parts/allocation: (a) three features with development, 2 each = 6. (b) Receipt evidence 2, cloth-cost mechanism 2, residual evidence with cost limitation 2, unchanged foreign-price/demand distinction 1 = 7. (c) Complete costs 2, capacity/demand 2, exchange uncertainty 1, conditional judgement 2 = 7.

items.prompt: A bicycle-parts business has N$8,000 in a payment account and needs to pay a supplier in another town. It also considers an equipment loan requiring fixed monthly repayments while sales vary seasonally. The owner mistakenly expects the central bank to provide the ordinary business account. (a) Define a commercial bank (2). (b) Explain two benefits of using a suitable payment account (4). (c) Explain how bank lending might affect the firm’s production and financial position (7). (d) Discuss whether the loan should be accepted simply because finance is offered (7).
items.canonical_answer: (a) Bank providing deposit, payment and lending services to customers. (b) Funds can be transferred to the distant supplier without transporting cash. Records can help the firm track payments and reconcile receipts. (c) Loan funds may allow equipment to be acquired sooner and enable additional production. Repayments and charges create obligations, so seasonal sales may leave a shortfall in low months even if annual sales appear adequate. The bank assesses its own risk; its offer does not remove the firm’s business risk. (d) The loan can help when suitable equipment generates enough receipts to support obligations. Against acceptance without analysis, finance has costs and the business has variable sales. The firm should compare realistic monthly cash availability with the exact loan terms, keeping resources for normal operations. Accept if a cautious seasonal scenario is affordable and productive use is demonstrated; otherwise negotiate different terms, reduce the purchase or delay. The central bank/commercial bank distinction should be corrected before seeking retail services.
marking_guidance: Context: bicycle parts. Parts/allocation: (a) customer bank 1, services 1. (b) distance payment and records, benefit + case effect 2 each = 4. (c) productive mechanism 3, repayment/seasonality 3, lender versus borrower risk 1 = 7. (d) productive benefit 2, cost/risk 2, condition-based judgement using monthly affordability 3 = 7.

items.prompt: Evaluate whether a village market should replace all cash payments with electronic payments when many customers use bank accounts, connectivity sometimes fails and several customers have no suitable payment device (9).
items.canonical_answer: Argument for: transfers can reduce carrying and counting cash and can provide records useful to sellers. Distance payments may make ordering more convenient and reduce cash transport. Argument against: unreliable connectivity can interrupt exchange; customers without suitable access may be excluded. Facilities and transaction charges may be costly relative to small purchases, and electronic instructions require careful authentication. Judgement: introduce electronic payments alongside a practical alternative rather than immediately relying on them for every sale. The condition for wider reliance is reliable access for the relevant customers at affordable cost. Acceptance and functioning facilities determine whether portability gains are useful; the availability of a device alone is insufficient.
marking_guidance: Argument for: convenience/records/transport mechanisms, up to 4. Argument against: connectivity/access/cost with effects, up to 4. Judgement: distinct condition on reliability and inclusion, 1. Total 9.

items.canonical_answer: (a) Unjustified unequal work treatment on a prohibited or irrelevant personal basis rather than relevant requirements. (b) Status-based exclusion requires fair opportunity and relevant rights assessment. The machine report requires investigation and correction of physical risk. (c) A poster can share information but does not itself resolve exclusion or make the machine safe. Actual assessment and a relevant complaint/enforcement route are needed for the work decision, while effective hazard correction requires action. No remedy or safety result follows merely from display. (d) Address the two issues separately through relevant protection channels, a fair work-based decision process and targeted safety investigation. Education can complement rather than replace these actions. The judgement prioritises actual risk reduction and fair treatment with appropriate evidence, without promising a legal outcome or making diagnosis-based assumptions.

items.prompt: Evaluate whether an authority should judge business protection effective solely because every firm receives a new information leaflet, with no evidence about understanding, behaviour or harm (9).
items.canonical_answer: For: clear information can help firms and users understand duties, risks and relevant routes, providing a useful starting point. Against: receipt is not understanding or compliance; physical hazards and unfair decisions may remain. Enforcement and adjustment need resources, and a leaflet may not match the main obstacle. Judgement: combine appropriate information with evidence on actual conduct and outcomes, using targeted follow-up where needed. The condition for an effectiveness claim is that the measure changes the relevant harmful process or improves meaningful access to protection, rather than distribution numbers alone.
marking_guidance: Argument for: information mechanism, up to 4. Argument against: implementation/harm and cost limits, up to 4. Judgement: distinct changed-conduct/outcome condition, 1. Total 9.

items.prompt: The Harbour Linen firm employs 40 workers. Thirty support a union proposal for a predictable rota, safety training and a pay review. Management reports falling orders and says immediate large pay increases are unaffordable. Staff complaints currently arrive separately. (a) Describe three aims shown by the proposal (6). (b) Examine the effects union representation could have in this firm (7). (c) Suggest a negotiating approach suitable for these circumstances (7).
items.canonical_answer: (a) A predictable rota improves working conditions by making hours more certain. Safety training seeks to reduce workplace danger. The pay review seeks improved rewards, though review does not assure an increase. (b) Combining complaints gives management a clearer common concern and can reduce repeated individual disputes. Safety cooperation could reduce avoidable injury and interruption. However, thirty supporters do not establish agreement from all forty. Falling orders constrain funds; costly demands or disruption could worsen the firm’s position and workers’ earnings. (c) Representatives should gather evidence on rota problems and discuss training costs with management, then negotiate affordable immediate improvements and a dated pay review linked to evidence of orders and resources. This addresses urgent conditions without assuming money exists. Members should receive the proposal before agreeing it. A delayed review risks postponing pay gains, so the timetable and information needed for review should be clear.
marking_guidance: Context: Harbour Linen. Parts and allocation, with bargaining mechanism and feasibility judgement: (a) Three aims: rota certainty, safety, reward review; 1 identification + 1 contextual development each = 6. (b) Clearer voice/communication up to 3, safety cooperation up to 2, membership or financial constraint up to 2 = 7. (c) Evidence collection/consultation 2, feasible staged negotiation 3, reasoned review safeguard 2 = 7.

items.prompt: (a) Define collective bargaining (2). (b) Define an employers’ association (2). (c) Explain one non-pay union aim (2). (c) Safer conditions reduce exposure to injury. (d) Advice helps organise the complaint for a fairer hearing. (e) Craft means a common skilled trade, which may involve manual work. (h) Acceptance depends on employer resources and the negotiated agreement, not the union’s aim alone.

items.prompt: A joinery firm employs trained machine operators and office staff. A worker union proposes shared safety training after repeated minor injuries. The employer is a member of a workshop owners’ association offering employment advice. Training would stop production for one morning; no estimate of longer-term savings is available. (a) Define a trade union (2). (b) Explain two ways the employers’ association could help the cooperative (4). (c) Explain how union involvement in safety training could affect workers and the firm (7). (d) Discuss whether the firm should accept the proposal (7).
items.canonical_answer: (a) Organisation representing workers in dealings with employers. (b) It can pool employment expertise so the cooperative prepares negotiations better. It can share members’ experience of scheduling training, helping limit interruption. (c) Representatives can collect evidence about injuries and explain staff concerns, helping target training. Better procedures may reduce injury, protecting workers and reducing future absence. Consultation can build confidence that concerns are heard. The firm loses a morning’s production, and training cannot by itself remove every hazard; equipment condition matters too. (d) Acceptance has a strong safety case given repeated injuries and could avoid continuing disruption. Against it, the immediate stoppage has an opportunity cost and no quantified savings are supplied. Accept appropriately targeted training while checking equipment and agreeing a less disruptive time. This judgement prioritises known safety concerns, with effectiveness reviewed afterwards rather than assuming the unmeasured savings exceed the cost.
marking_guidance: Context: joinery. Parts and allocation: (a) Organisation 1, worker representation 1. (b) Shared advice and practical experience, each action + consequence 2 = 4. (c) Evidence targeting 2, reduced injuries/absence 3, communication or limits 2 = 7. (d) Safety case 2, production cost/uncertain savings 2, conditional decision including equipment/timing/review 3 = 7. Mechanism: representation targets training; judgement considers the known injuries against uncertain savings.

items.prompt: Evaluate whether a regional group of seasonal workers should form an active union when workers are dispersed, shared transport concerns are serious and subscriptions would be a noticeable household expense (9).
items.canonical_answer: For: a shared organisation could document transport problems across sites and negotiate common arrangements, giving isolated workers a clearer voice. Pooled subscriptions could fund communication and advice that each worker could not easily afford separately. Against: distance makes meetings and consultation costly, while subscriptions reduce income immediately. Low participation or differing shifts could prevent a workable common proposal; membership alone cannot compel employers to fund transport. Judgement: formation is worthwhile if a realistic communication plan and affordable subscriptions can sustain participation around the shared transport concern. Begin with representative consultation and a costed transport proposal, then review whether the benefit warrants continued contributions. The decisive condition is effective representation of dispersed members rather than the size of the membership list alone.
marking_guidance: Argument for: shared evidence/voice and pooled resources, up to 4. Argument against: organising cost, subscriptions and uncertain implementation, up to 4. Judgement: distinct feasible participation/affordability condition, 1. Total 9.

items.prompt: An economy has real income N$120 million and 20,000 people, later N$126 million and 21,000. A service-access average improves, but a remote group remains poorly served. No distribution or quality details are supplied. (a) Describe three relevant features (6). (b) Examine what the measures show about living standards (7). (c) Suggest a better evidence-based comparison (7).
items.canonical_answer: (a) Real total rises 5 percent. Population also rises 5 percent. Income per head stays N$6,000 while the aggregate access measure and local experience differ. (b) More total resources do not show a higher average per person. The service average can improve without equivalent gains for the remote group. Distribution, quality and reliability are missing, so individual welfare improvements cannot be inferred. (c) Compare consistent per-person measures and group access, then examine reliability, quality and relevant education/health conditions. The judgement recognises the recorded aggregate changes while asking whether gains reach people meaningfully, rather than dismissing or overstating the indicators.
marking_guidance: Context: economy. Parts/allocation: (a) total, population, average/access 2 each=6. (b) ratio mechanism 3, distribution/service limits 4=7. (c) comparable data 3, wider outcomes 2, conditional judgement 2=7. Mechanism: access and distribution determine usable benefits; judgement requires actual group outcomes.

items.prompt: A region provides digital public information. Connected residents save journeys, but some households cannot afford access and training support is limited. The authority proposes declaring improved living standards solely from device numbers. (a) Define the digital divide (2). (b) Explain two possible benefits of usable technology (4). (c) Explain why effects differ between households (7). (d) Discuss the proposed success measure (7).
items.canonical_answer: (a) Unequal access to or ability to use information technology/services. (b) Useful remote information can save travel and make assistance easier to reach. Communication can support learning or productive opportunities when relevant and usable. (c) Affordability, reliability and skills constrain use, so a device count can coexist with exclusion. The connected group gains convenience while others may lose a practical route if alternatives disappear. Real outcomes also depend on the information’s usefulness and ability to act. (d) Device numbers describe an input, not full meaningful access or welfare. Measure use, service reliability, costs and outcomes across groups. Declare a supported improvement where actual benefits reach intended residents at an acceptable resource cost, retaining alternatives for those excluded; the count alone is insufficient.
marking_guidance: Context: digital service. Parts/allocation: (a) unequal access 1, use capability 1. (b) two opportunity mechanisms 2 each=4. (c) cost/skills 3, distribution 2, usefulness 2=7. (d) count usefulness 2, missing outcome dimensions 2, conditional judgement 3=7. Mechanism: access and distribution determine usable benefits; judgement requires actual group outcomes.

items.prompt: Evaluate whether an analyst should describe living standards as uniformly high solely from a high national real-income-per-head figure (9).
items.canonical_answer: For: a high real average indicates substantial measured resources per person on the stated basis and can support useful consumption and services. Against: distribution, population groups, public access, education, survival and environmental conditions may differ. A mean is not each person’s income and a single dimension is incomplete. Judgement: use the real average as one relevant indicator alongside group distribution and non-income outcomes. The condition for a uniform claim is evidence about residents’ actual conditions across the relevant dimensions, which the average alone does not provide.
marking_guidance: Argument for: resource information up to 4. Argument against: distribution/non-income limits up to 4. Judgement: distinct group-and-dimension evidence condition 1. Total 9. Condition: comparable evidence across people and dimensions must support the wider claim.

blocks.heading: Employment and what a count omits
blocks.text:
Employment concerns participation in work for pay or profit under the stated measurement convention. A person can be an employee or work in their own business. In a data task, use the definition and reference period supplied rather than invent an official hour threshold. An employment count records people, not the total hours they work or the money they receive. Two people can each count as employed while having very different hours and rewards.

For a community, a part-time worker and a full-time worker may each be included under the given rules. Their combined headcount is two, but that does not mean their labour hours equal two full-time schedules. If the question concerns productive input, hours may provide additional information. If it concerns employment access, people counted can be the relevant measure. A higher employment total also does not prove improved job security, safer work or higher productivity. Those are separate dimensions requiring evidence. A fair comparison keeps the reference population and period consistent. Changing the measurement rule can change a count without an equivalent change in actual work. This is why a trend explanation should distinguish economic change from a change in how the data are collected or defined.

Consider a worker who remains employed but has hours cut from forty to twenty per week. The employment count is unchanged while paid time and likely earnings fall under the stated hourly arrangement. This shows why headcount alone is not a complete account of labour use or welfare. Another dataset might record the hours change directly. Use whichever measures are supplied without pretending a missing dimension has been observed.

blocks.heading: Unemployment and the labour-force boundary
blocks.text:
Unemployment concerns people of working age who are willing and able to work, seeking it but unable to find it, subject to the stated convention. Not every person outside employment meets those conditions. A person choosing not to seek paid work is different from an active job seeker without an opportunity. Students, carers or retired people should not be automatically assigned a status without the relevant facts and rules; some may also be working or seeking work.

A dataset explicitly classifies 600 employed and 150 unemployed people in a labour force of 750. The unemployment rate is 150 divided by 750 times 100, or 20 percent. If the working-age population is 1,000, dividing 150 by 1,000 gives 15 percent, a different population ratio rather than the stated labour-force unemployment rate. The denominator matters. A lower unemployment rate can also result when job seekers leave the labour force, not only when they find jobs. A count of unemployment, its rate and the level of employment should therefore be read together. The data do not by themselves identify cyclical, structural, seasonal or frictional causes; those require evidence about demand, mismatch, timing and search. Keep the classification boundary separate from the explanation of how someone arrived in that position.

A measurement task should say which criteria apply. Some official statistics use different search or availability definitions. The exercises explicitly provide the classification so the learner can practise the denominator. A comparison between sources would need consistent definitions before rates could be ranked fairly. A difference caused by classification should not be misreported as a new job or a loss of work.

blocks.heading: Participation and consistent comparisons
blocks.text:
Labour force participation means involvement in the labour force, comprising employed people and those classified as unemployed. The participation rate compares that labour force with the relevant working-age population. Using the figures, 750 out of 1,000 gives 75 percent participation. This is not the 20 percent unemployment rate, because the numerators and denominators answer different questions. Participation asks how many are in the labour market; unemployment asks how many within it lack work under the definition.

A rise in participation can occur when people begin seeking work before a job is found, increasing labour-force numbers without an immediate employment gain. A fall can reflect retirement, study, caring choices or discouraged search, depending on the evidence. Do not assume the same explanation for each change. If a task states that twenty job seekers stop seeking and no one gains work, unemployment and participation counts change even though employment does not rise. Such an example shows why one favourable-looking rate cannot replace a full account. This links the measurement unit to the main employment-pattern discussion: use a common reference population and period, label the rate and then explain what changes. A conclusion about access to work needs the relevant status movements rather than a percentage considered in isolation. A change in working-age population also affects participation rates even if labour-force numbers are unchanged. Keep numerator and denominator visible when explaining the direction. This is a ratio interpretation, rather than a prediction about why people make participation choices.

blocks.heading: Levels and patterns
blocks.text:
Employment level means the number in work, while employment pattern describes how work is distributed across activities, groups or arrangements. A comparison might concern agriculture, manufacturing and services, working hours or employment among particular population groups. The level and the pattern can change in different directions. If a sector employs more people but the whole workforce expands faster, its employment share can fall. State whether a claim concerns a count or a proportion before describing the trend.

In an economy, manufacturing employs 200 of 1,000 employed people, a 20 percent share. Later it employs 240 of 1,500, a 16 percent share. Manufacturing jobs rise by 40 while its share falls four percentage points. This does not show forty jobs disappeared. Nor does a larger service share necessarily mean more productive jobs or higher wages; job quality, hours and skills require separate evidence. Technology, demand, education, location and policy can influence patterns. A description should use the actual data, while an explanation should state the mechanism and its evidence rather than infer a cause solely from the sector label. These are example figures.

A level can change while the composition stays the same. If every sector’s employment rises by the same proportion, their shares can remain unchanged. Conversely, workers can shift between activities while total employment stays constant. This provides two different counterexamples to treating level and pattern as synonyms. An explanation should also distinguish employment shifts from output shifts: a sector can produce more with fewer workers if productivity changes. That relationship requires output and input evidence, rather than following from the employment count alone.

Employment is often grouped into three sectors: primary (extracting natural resources, such as farming, fishing and mining), secondary (manufacturing and construction) and tertiary (services such as retail, banking, tourism and government services). As an economy develops, the share of workers in the primary sector usually falls, the secondary share first rises, and the tertiary sector eventually employs the largest share. Mechanisation of farming and rising incomes, which increase demand for services, help explain this. Other changing patterns include more women in paid work, more part-time and temporary jobs, more self-employment and informal-sector work, and changes in the share of public-sector employment.

blocks.heading: Causes need diagnosis
blocks.text:
Labour demand is the number of workers employers are willing and able to employ at each wage rate over a period. It is a derived demand, because it depends on demand for the goods and services the workers produce. A general fall in spending can reduce orders and labour demand, while a change in technology can reduce demand for some tasks even where other vacancies exist. A tourism season can create predictable fluctuations, and normal job search takes time. These mechanisms are called cyclical, structural, seasonal and frictional unemployment respectively, explained in their own sections. Reasons for high unemployment in a country include: a fall in total demand during a recession; mechanisation and new technology replacing workers; a mismatch between the education or skills of job seekers and the jobs available; a labour force growing faster than new jobs because of rapid population growth; low investment by firms; cheaper imports replacing local production; seasonal work in farming, fishing and tourism; and wages set above the level at which employers will hire all job seekers.

An investigation should identify the initial change and the barrier to work. A closed business does not by itself prove which mechanism applies: was its market generally weak, its product replaced, its active season over or its workers between jobs? The appropriate response depends on the answer. Skills, transport, information and the availability of vacancies can interact. A person may face more than one obstacle, so categories support analysis rather than force the case into an unsupported single label. Avoid assuming unwillingness to work from the absence of a job. The unemployment definition concerns people meeting stated criteria, while a cause explanation needs the relevant economic evidence.

blocks.heading: Consequences for households and the economy
blocks.text:
Unemployment can reduce household earnings and spending capacity, depending on savings, other household income and support. Prolonged exclusion from work can weaken skills, confidence or future access, though effects vary by person and circumstances. A job loss is not a measure of someone’s value or effort. The economic explanation should trace the lost employment to resources and opportunities rather than blame an individual for a market condition.

At economy level, suitable idle labour can mean forgone output: production that feasible use of those resources could have created. Actual vacancies, complementary resources and organisation matter to that potential. Lower earnings can reduce tax receipts and spending on firms’ products, while greater need for support can pressure public resources. These consequences can reinforce weak demand, but do not occur in identical amounts for each household. A family losing its main wage may reduce non-essential purchases, affecting local sellers. Health or social difficulties are possible consequences of hardship, not an inevitable property of unemployed people. Compare the stated household and economy conditions, and distinguish forgone potential from output that has actually been produced.

Duration and access to alternatives affect consequences. A short search supported by savings may have different immediate effects from a prolonged gap in a household with no other income. The distinction does not make either person’s experience unimportant; it identifies the resources relevant to the mechanism. Public support can cushion spending but requires finance and administration. When comparing consequences, state which are direct lost-earnings effects, which follow through reduced spending and which remain possible longer-term effects needing additional evidence.

For the economy and the government, the main consequences are: lower output (GDP), because labour is a wasted resource; lower income-tax and VAT revenue; higher government spending on support for the unemployed; lower demand for firms’ products, which can cause further job losses; lower living standards; and skilled workers emigrating to find work. Social problems can also increase, but an answer should not repeat them as its only points.

blocks.heading: Matching a remedy to the barrier
blocks.text:
Remedies should address the evidenced cause. Demand support can help when suitable labour is idle because output orders are weak. Common remedies include: fiscal policy, where the government raises its spending (for example on roads and schools) or cuts taxes so that total demand and firms’ need for workers rise; monetary policy, where lower interest rates encourage borrowing and spending, although Namibia’s link to the rand limits how freely the Bank of Namibia can set rates (see 6.2); education and retraining so that workers’ skills match the vacancies; subsidies or tax relief for firms that create jobs; labour-intensive public works; encouraging local and foreign investment; and import duties that protect jobs in domestic industries, which can lead to higher prices and retaliation. Each remedy works best against a particular cause. Retraining may help workers whose skills no longer match available work. Better vacancy information can reduce search delays, while access or mobility support can matter when jobs are difficult to reach. Broader off-season activity can reduce a recurring seasonal gap. Each has resource requirements and limits. Providing a course without relevant vacancies or a feasible access route does not guarantee employment.

For a coastal service with off-season job gaps, a general recruitment website may improve information but cannot by itself create customers in the quiet period. Developing feasible alternative services could be more relevant, though demand and skills must support them. In a case of unfilled technical jobs alongside job seekers lacking the required expertise, training can address the specific mismatch if it is appropriate and accessible. It uses time and resources and completion is not an employment promise.

A supported policy judgement names the main obstacle, explains the response, considers cost and states a condition for success. This links to occupational mobility in 4.1, earnings and skills in 4.2 and government policy in 6.2. Measure achieved suitable employment rather than merely the number enrolled or the amount spent. A combination may be justified when several barriers are evidenced, but avoid listing policies without showing how each addresses the case. The time horizon also matters: a suitable course takes time to produce skills, while urgent household needs may exist immediately. Separate short-term support from the longer-term route into feasible work. A recommendation can acknowledge uncertainty without becoming vague. State the most supported diagnosis, name the evidence still needed and explain how that evidence would change the choice. If available vacancies require skills but their location is unknown, training may be relevant while the access conclusion remains conditional. This preserves a useful next action without inventing a successful placement.

blocks.heading: Cyclical unemployment
blocks.text:
Cyclical unemployment arises when weak aggregate demand during a downturn reduces employers’ need for labour. Firms facing fewer orders may reduce output, hours or jobs. The initial problem concerns demand for products and the derived demand for workers, rather than a sudden disappearance of workers’ skills. A general decline across activities is more consistent with this mechanism than a recurring off-season gap at one service, though evidence is still needed.

A repair-and-construction economy experiences broad postponed spending and lower orders while trained workers and equipment remain available. Demand-support measures may help firms use those resources if implemented effectively. Extra spending does not necessarily solve a simultaneous skills shortage elsewhere, and capacity constraints can limit the response. The policy case therefore depends on useful idle resources and the nature of demand weakness. An individual firm losing customers to a new technology is not automatically a cyclical event simply because it cuts jobs. Classify by cause. Explain the chain from lower spending to fewer orders, reduced output need and then labour demand, keeping the actors and period clear. This shows why supporting general demand may be more relevant than retraining everyone for a problem caused mainly by a temporary downturn. It also leaves room for additional measures when a case supplies more than one obstacle. A broad fall in product orders should be distinguished from one employer losing market share to another local firm. In the latter case jobs might move between employers rather than disappear across the whole economy. The case needs evidence about the wider demand change before a general cyclical conclusion is supported.

blocks.heading: Structural unemployment
blocks.text:
Structural unemployment arises from a persistent mismatch between available workers and the types or locations of work demanded. Changes in technology, industry or trading patterns can reduce the usefulness of some existing tasks while other jobs require different expertise or are elsewhere. The problem is not necessarily a shortage of all vacancies. Workers may be willing to work but unable to move immediately into the available roles because skills, costs or access do not match.

A manual records operation contracts while employers seek electronic-system technicians. Retraining may help if the courses teach relevant skills, applicants can access and complete them, and real work opportunities exist. Mobility support or information can also matter where location is the barrier. These approaches use time and resources, and no programme can promise each participant an offer. Raising general demand alone may leave the mismatch unresolved, though it could help a separate demand problem. This contrasts structural with cyclical unemployment. A seasonal return of the same activity is different again: the initial difficulty there follows a recurring calendar pattern. In a supplied case, identify what changed in the job structure, which requirement the workers lack and what feasible remedy addresses that requirement. A technology label alone is insufficient if the case does not actually show a mismatch. Skill and location barriers can interact. Training may create relevant expertise while distant vacancies remain inaccessible because moving or travel is costly. That makes access support a possible complement, subject to feasibility. A single course should not be presented as solving the whole problem if the prompt explicitly supplies an additional barrier.

blocks.heading: Seasonal unemployment
blocks.text:
Seasonal unemployment arises from predictable seasonal changes in labour demand. Agriculture, visitor services or other activities may need more workers at particular times and fewer in the quiet period. The recurrence is the distinguishing feature. A generally shrinking industry is not made seasonal merely because a job loss happens during one month. State the link between the period and the activity’s demand.

A visitor-camp service employs more staff in its busy season and fewer afterwards. If workers seeking employment cannot find other work in the quiet period, the case can illustrate seasonal unemployment. Their skills have not necessarily become obsolete, and a broad national downturn is not required. Possible responses include developing feasible off-season activities, skills useful in more than one season or better information about complementary work. Each depends on actual demand, resources and access. Relabelling the same vacant period as a training course does not itself create a paid job. Alternative work may also be distant or require different expertise. A policy judgement should examine those constraints rather than promise that diversification removes the gap. Compare the recurring timing with structural mismatch and cyclical weakness to show why the selected cause fits. This keeps the explanation tied to evidence instead of guessing from the sector name alone. The recurring period provides a useful discriminating test: ask whether the same activity normally returns when the season changes. If the market instead contracts persistently because the product is replaced, the evidence points towards a structural change. Neither label should be assigned solely from the calendar date of dismissal.

blocks.heading: Frictional unemployment
blocks.text:
Frictional unemployment is temporary joblessness during search and transition between jobs or entry into work. Even where suitable opportunities exist, finding information, applying and agreeing a match takes time. The cause is not automatically a persistent mismatch or a broad lack of demand. A person leaving one job and searching for another can illustrate the mechanism when the relevant work is available and the difficulty is the matching interval.

Better vacancy information, clear requirements and efficient matching may shorten search. These measures do not by themselves create missing skills or additional orders. A qualified technician learns late about a suitable local vacancy; improved information could address that particular delay. If no such job exists, the same explanation would be insufficient. The policy should fit the actual barrier. Frictional does not mean the person is making no effort or that their income loss is unimportant. A short period can still be difficult depending on savings and commitments. This links the cause categories back to consequences and remedies: identify the initial change, the labour-market obstacle and how the proposed measure can alter it. Cyclical, structural, seasonal and frictional causes can overlap in a complex case, so a justified answer may state which is best supported and what additional evidence would distinguish alternatives. A classification is strongest when it explains the facts, rather than repeating a memorised label. Efficient matching still involves evaluating suitability. Faster information is helpful when it reaches people who can perform the work and realistically access it. Counting website visits or applications is not the same as achieved employment, so the evaluation needs the outcome and the barrier it was intended to remove.

topics/5.1/content-units/CU-6145-5.1.jso.title: The private firm as producer and employer — 5.1

blocks.heading: Profit as an objective
blocks.text:
Profit is total revenue minus total cost over a stated period. Profit maximisation means producing the output that gives the highest possible profit (total revenue minus total cost). Marginal revenue (MR) is the extra revenue from selling one more unit; marginal cost (MC) is the extra cost of producing one more unit. While MR is greater than MC, each extra unit adds more to revenue than to cost, so profit rises. Once MC is greater than MR, an extra unit reduces profit. In the usual model, profit is highest where MC = MR and extra units change from adding to profit (MR > MC) to reducing it (MC > MR). Equality alone is not enough if the change goes the other way. It differs from maximising output or sales revenue. A firm can sell more while adding costs that exceed the extra receipts. It can also reduce output and improve profit if the forgone sales would have cost more to supply than they earned. The comparison requires both sides of the calculation and a consistent period.

Suppose a cabinet maker has two complete monthly plans. Plan A gives revenue N$30,000 and total cost N$24,000, leaving N$6,000 profit. Plan B gives revenue N$35,000 and total cost N$30,000, leaving N$5,000. A yields N$1,000 more profit despite lower revenue. These figures describe complete stated plans, so the comparison is supported. If a case instead lists only material cost, do not subtract it and call the remainder profit: wages, premises or other costs may be missing. Use the information actually supplied and label a partial comparison accordingly.
