blocks.heading: From a schedule to curves
blocks.text:
Demand and supply schedules describe planned purchases and sales at different prices during a stated period. Quantities need units and a time period: packets per week differs from packets held in a storeroom. A demand curve shows the buyer relationship and a supply curve the producer relationship. Conventionally put price on the vertical axis and quantity per period on the horizontal axis. Label the curves D and S, attach units to the axes and use one consistent scale. Each plotted point is a price-quantity pair, not an arbitrary mark on the page.

For a simple market in seed packets, use prices N$10, N$20 and N$30 per packet. Quantities demanded per week are respectively 90, 60 and 30; quantities supplied are 30, 60 and 90. Plot demand coordinates as (quantity, price): (90,10), (60,20), (30,30). Supply points are (30,10), (60,20), (90,30). Join each set with a straight line for this simple example. Demand slopes down (the law of demand): at a lower price more buyers can afford the product and some switch to it from alternatives. Supply slopes up (the law of supply): a higher price makes production more profitable, so firms offer more. The data are illustrative relationships, not a claim about every real market. Moving from N$10 to N$20 along these schedules reduces quantity demanded and increases quantity supplied while other relevant conditions remain unchanged.

Check the placement of coordinates before joining points. At a price of N$10, the demand quantity 90 belongs at horizontal coordinate 90 and vertical coordinate 10. Reversing the axes while leaving the labels unchanged would misrepresent the schedule. The supply point at that same price is at horizontal coordinate 30. The horizontal distance between them therefore represents a quantity difference at one price. A vertical distance instead represents a price difference at one quantity. Reading the units makes these two comparisons easier to keep separate.
blocks.repair_note: Step-6 Claude review: added standard examined content (named points, definitions, lists) missing from notes; corrected definition cards and template-garbled answers; removed author/tooling wording and invented/original labels.

blocks.heading: Movements along both curves
blocks.text:
A second schedule shows the same shapes. At N$8, N$12 and N$16, buyers want 80, 60 and 40 units a week and sellers offer 40, 60 and 80. As the price rises from N$8 to N$16, quantity demanded falls along D and quantity supplied rises along S; neither curve shifts.

![Demand and supply curves with movements along both](diagrams/item-6145-3.2-002-proc-answer.png)

blocks.heading: Equilibrium and adjustment
blocks.text:
Equilibrium price is the price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied. In the seed-packet schedule it is N$20, where both equal 60 packets per week. Mark the intersection E, then project to the axes to show the equilibrium price and quantity. Equality matters: a high quantity or a price acceptable to one trader alone does not establish equilibrium. Equilibrium also does not mean every consumer obtains all they would like at no cost; it concerns planned quantities at the stated market price.

At N$10, buyers want 90 packets while sellers offer 30, producing excess demand of 60 packets per week. Excess demand is also called a shortage, and excess supply a surplus. A movement along the demand curve caused by a fall in price is an extension of demand; one caused by a rise in price is a contraction. Competition for limited offers can put upward pressure on price. As price rises along unchanged curves, quantity demanded falls and quantity supplied rises. At N$30, supply of 90 exceeds demand of 30, leaving excess supply of 60 and downward pressure on price. In the basic model prices can adjust towards N$20.

![Equilibrium at N$20 and the shortage at N$10](diagrams/item-6145-3.2-006-proc-answer.png)

Real adjustment may take time, and regulation or contractual arrangements can prevent free movement. A controlled price below equilibrium would be drawn as a horizontal price line below E, not as a new demand curve. Price control changes the permitted price; its imposition alone does not establish that buyers’ tastes or producers’ costs changed.
blocks.repair_note: Revision-01 visual authoring: worked diagram image reference added for ITEM-6145-3.2-006-PROC; text otherwise unchanged

blocks.heading: Shifts and their causes
blocks.text:
A movement along a curve follows a change in the product’s own price, other relevant conditions unchanged. A shift follows a change in another determinant, so the quantity at a given price changes. Higher income may raise demand for a normal good; changes in preferences, population and related-product prices can also shift demand. The direction depends on the relationship. If tea and a herbal drink are substitutes, a higher tea price may increase demand for the herbal drink. If two products are used together, a higher price of one can reduce demand for the other. Name two distinct alternatives when giving a substitute pair: a named type of bread and bread as its whole category do not provide two separate alternatives.

Supply determinants concern producers’ willingness and ability to offer output. Higher input costs can reduce supply, while improved technology can increase it. Weather can affect agricultural output, and entry or exit of producers can change market supply. Explain the channel rather than assigning a factor by its name alone. A household income change directly concerns buyers; a rise in the cost of cloth concerns suppliers of clothing. Demand-shift factors also differ from determinants of price responsiveness. The availability of close substitutes helps explain responsiveness to a product’s own price; a change in tastes can instead move the entire demand curve. Responsiveness is developed in topic 3.3, so do not treat a shift as evidence that elasticity has increased.

When the term price elasticity is used, its categories include elastic, inelastic, unit elastic and perfectly inelastic demand. These describe responsiveness, not a choice between a rightward and a leftward shift. Their definitions and calculations belong to topic 3.3. A change in tastes alone does not supply the price-and-quantity evidence needed to select a responsiveness category. Holding the distinction clear here prevents the same word change being used for two different analytical questions.

Demand increases (shifts right) when: income rises, for a normal good (for an inferior good, such as a cheap staple that people buy less of as they become richer, demand falls instead); the price of a substitute rises; the price of a complement falls (complements are in joint demand because they are used together, such as torches and batteries); tastes move in the product’s favour or advertising succeeds; the population grows; or buyers expect prices to rise soon. Supply increases (shifts right) when: costs of production fall; technology improves; the government gives a subsidy or cuts an indirect tax such as VAT; good weather raises harvests; or more firms enter the market. The opposite changes shift each curve to the left. State whether each factor increases or decreases demand or supply.

blocks.heading: A demand increase
blocks.text:
Keep the original seed-packet supply schedule. Now suppose more households begin home gardening, and demand at N$10, N$20 and N$30 becomes 120, 90 and 60 packets per week. Plot the new demand curve D1 through (120,10), (90,20), (60,30), to the right of D0. At the old N$20 price, demand is now 90 but supply remains 60, so excess demand is 30. This puts upward pressure on price if it can adjust. The new intersection lies at N$25 and 75 packets per week: on the straight-line schedules, demand and supply both equal 75 there.

Show E0 at (60,20) and E1 at (75,25), with axis projections for both.

![Demand increase from D0 to D1 with E0 and E1](diagrams/item-6145-3.2-010-proc-answer.png)

Demand has shifted, but the price adjustment creates a movement along the unchanged supply curve. It would be wrong to shift supply simply because producers offer more at the higher price. The new equilibrium has both higher price and higher quantity because buyers demand more at each price while the supply relationship is unchanged. The direction can be explained without calculating a slope: compare the old and new curves, identify the imbalance at the old price, then trace the adjustment towards the new intersection.
blocks.repair_note: Revision-01 visual authoring: worked diagram image reference added for ITEM-6145-3.2-010-PROC; text otherwise unchanged

blocks.heading: A supply change and competing effects
blocks.text:
Return to the original demand curve and consider improved production methods that raise supply by 30 packets at each listed price. New supply at N$10, N$20 and N$30 is 60, 90 and 120. Plot S1 to the right of S0. At the old N$20 price, supply is 90 and demand is 60, leaving excess supply of 30. Price tends downwards; the new equilibrium is N$15 and 75 packets per week.

![Supply increase from S0 to S1 with E0 and E1](diagrams/item-6145-3.2-017-proc-answer.png)

This is a supply increase, not a reduction, because more is offered at the same price. The demand curve stays in place while quantity demanded rises along it as price falls.

A supply reduction works in the opposite direction: with demand unchanged, price tends to rise and equilibrium quantity to fall. If both demand and supply increase, quantity rises in the basic model but the direction of price depends on the relative shifts. Stronger demand pushes price upwards, while stronger supply pushes it downwards. Without magnitudes, a definite net price claim would be unsupported. This gives a useful analysis sequence: identify the affected side and determinant, state the shift, compare quantities at the old price, then locate the new equilibrium. Connect this reasoning to productivity in topic 5.2 for production changes and to advertising in topic 3.4 for changes in buyer information or preferences. A diagram supports the mechanism only when its labels, direction and written conclusion agree.

A price rise and a quantity fall together are consistent with a supply reduction when demand is unchanged. A price rise and a quantity rise are consistent with a demand increase when supply is unchanged. These comparisons help interpret a supplied case, but observations alone do not prove the unchanged conditions. A real event may affect both sides. For example, a local festival may attract more buyers while temporary transport problems restrict deliveries. Explain both changes if the case supplies them, then state what additional information is needed for a definite net conclusion. Do not use the convenience of a simple diagram to erase a stated second change. A conclusion should state the comparison explicitly: price relative to the original equilibrium, quantity relative to the original equilibrium, and which conditions were held unchanged. This keeps a correct curve shift connected to its economic meaning.

blocks.heading: Demand is willing and able buying
blocks.text:
Demand means the quantities buyers are willing and able to buy at different prices over a stated period, other relevant conditions unchanged. Wanting an expensive product without the ability to pay does not constitute effective demand at that price. Ability alone is also insufficient if the person chooses not to buy. The definition brings willingness and ability together. State the period because buying ten loaves each week differs from buying ten loaves each month.

A demand schedule describes several possible quantities at different prices, rather than a single purchase. In a simple example, a household buys six packets per month at N$12 each but four at N$18, with its income and preferences unchanged. That is a movement between quantities on the same demand relationship. If a change in the household’s circumstances causes it to buy more at both prices, the relationship itself has changed. This distinction avoids saying demand increased merely because a lower price encouraged a larger purchase. For a market, the quantities bought by relevant buyers can be combined at each price. Do not add quantities referring to different prices as though they were simultaneous purchases at one market price. The curve is a set of alternatives under stated conditions, not a pile of quantities to be summed across the price axis.

The willingness-and-ability test also explains why a survey of wishes is not a complete demand schedule. Respondents might like a product while being unable or unwilling to purchase it at the listed price. A useful schedule specifies the product, price, quantity and period under relevant conditions. It can concern one buyer or a whole market, so state which is meant before interpreting a quantity. A change in market buyer numbers can alter market demand even if each existing buyer’s schedule is unchanged.

blocks.heading: Supply is planned offering
blocks.text:
Supply means the quantities producers are willing and able to offer at different prices over a stated period, other relevant conditions unchanged. A producer might possess inputs but lack the capacity to produce more immediately. It might also hold output but choose not to offer all of it at the current price. Supply therefore concerns planned offers under stated conditions, rather than physical stock alone. An existing inventory records what is held at a point in time; weekly supply records a flow offered during a period.

For a soap workshop, a higher selling price may make additional weekly output worthwhile, provided inputs and capacity allow it. The workshop moves along its existing supply curve when its own product price changes and other relevant conditions stay the same. If a new process reduces the resources needed per bar, more may be offered at each price, shifting supply. The words more output are insufficient to distinguish the two cases: explain why the planned quantity changes. A seller choosing an asking price does not establish that buyers will purchase the entire offer. Demand and supply are separate plans, and their equality identifies equilibrium. This links these definitions back to the market diagram: price belongs on the vertical axis, quantities per period on the horizontal axis, and the labels identify buyer or producer plans rather than actual sales assumed in advance.

Capacity matters when interpreting producers’ plans. Higher prices can encourage more output, but a workshop already using its equipment fully may be unable to respond quickly. This does not change the definition of supply; it shows why the time period and production conditions belong in the explanation. Stocks can help a seller meet current orders, while future supply may depend on replenishment or new production. Avoid treating goods sitting in storage as necessarily offered for sale at every possible price.

blocks.heading: Male and female earnings
blocks.text:
A gender earnings gap is a measured difference between male and female earnings for a specified population and comparison basis. The measure might concern hourly rates, monthly earnings or annual receipts. These are not interchangeable. A monthly average can reflect hours worked as well as pay per hour, and an annual average can reflect periods without paid work. State which population and measure the data describe before explaining the result. This avoids treating an undefined gap as though it were one universal statistic.

Possible influences include occupation mix, experience, paid hours, career interruptions, access to education or promotion, caring responsibilities and discrimination. Their relevance must be established from evidence. Gender itself does not determine an individual’s skill, work effort or productivity. It would be unsound to explain a pay gap by assuming one gender is naturally more productive or uniformly prefers a particular job. A raw average also cannot show that discrimination is either the whole explanation or absent. To investigate, compare like work and relevant circumstances while recognising that unequal access to opportunities may itself affect the observed job mix. An example comparing average monthly earnings of male and female groups can illustrate measurement. The example shows the difference between a measured gap and its causes.

blocks.heading: Skills, training and scarcity
blocks.text:
A skill earnings differential compares rewards for work requiring different levels or kinds of acquired expertise. The shorthand skilled and unskilled concerns requirements of the work, rather than a judgement about a person’s worth or general ability. A job requiring less formal training can still involve effort, judgement and reliability. Longer training can limit the immediate supply of qualified workers, while the usefulness of the skill to employers affects demand. Both sides contribute to the possible pay difference.

A refrigeration technician may need training that few local applicants possess. If firms need the service and replacing the worker is difficult, scarcity can support higher pay. The explanation requires demand for the expertise as well as limited supply; a rare skill that employers do not need may attract little reward. Similarly, an experienced worker in a role requiring less formal training may earn more than a newly qualified worker elsewhere. Hours, bargaining and responsibility can reverse a simple comparison. When analysing a supplied case, trace training or expertise to availability and productive contribution, then to possible negotiating or recruitment pressure. Do not turn the tendency into a claim that every trained worker earns more than every worker in another category. The market and time period determine how strongly the influences operate.

blocks.heading: Public and private employment
blocks.text:
A public-private earnings comparison contrasts rewards in government-owned or controlled employment with rewards in privately owned employment. Ownership sector is different from occupation and from stage of production. Both sectors can employ clerical staff, drivers, managers and specialists. Comparing their overall averages without examining the job mix may therefore compare different types of work. A higher public-sector average in an illustrative dataset would not prove that the same individual would receive a higher rate for identical work merely by changing ownership sector.

Budgets, recruitment needs, pay structures, bargaining and institutional objectives can affect rewards in either sector. A public employer may use formal salary scales, while a private employer may link some payments to performance or commercial conditions; actual arrangements vary. These are possible explanatory mechanisms rather than universal rules. Neither ownership form guarantees higher pay, greater security or a particular bonus. If a case supplies differences in benefits or hours, include them in a fair comparison while distinguishing direct earnings from non-wage conditions. For a driver choosing between a public service and a private delivery business, the stated wage, hours, responsibilities and conditions provide a better basis than ownership labels alone. The explanation should identify why the particular employer needs the worker and what resources or arrangements shape its offer.

An overall average can change even when no existing worker’s rate changes. If an employer recruits several highly paid specialists, the average for its workforce may rise because its composition changed. This illustrates why a comparison across ownership sectors needs information about the people and jobs included. It does not show that one ownership form is intrinsically more generous or productive.

blocks.heading: Agriculture, manufacturing and services
blocks.text:
Sectoral earnings comparisons group rewards by economic activity. Agriculture concerns activities such as growing crops and raising livestock. Manufacturing transforms materials into products. Services provide activities such as repair, transport or teaching. Each broad sector contains varied occupations and business conditions. A sector average is therefore a summary, not a promise about the reward for a particular job. Services can include both highly specialised and less formally trained work, while agricultural and manufacturing businesses also employ specialists and managers.

Productivity, the demand for output, available skills, labour supply, seasonality and the mix of jobs can influence differences. Seasonal work may provide fewer paid weeks even if the hourly rate is similar. Equipment can raise output per worker, but the effect on earnings depends on demand, bargaining and how gains are shared. A factory’s higher average annual earnings than a seasonal farm’s might partly reflect steadier employment rather than a higher rate for each hour. Conversely, a specialist agricultural role may pay more than a routine manufacturing role. Explain the evidence supplied instead of arranging the three sectors in a fixed ladder. This links to productivity in 5.2 and employment in 7.2: activity, working time and skill composition help interpret earnings, while a label alone cannot establish either individual productivity or a fair wage comparison.

For a simple seasonal contrast, a worker paid for eight months and one paid for twelve months at the same monthly rate receive different annual totals. The shorter employment period can explain that difference without assuming unequal monthly rates. A complete account should distinguish rate, working time and availability of employment before comparing productive contribution or skill. The basis should remain consistent when comparing sectors or tracking the same sector through time.

blocks.heading: Economic rent
blocks.text:
Economic rent is the part of a factor’s reward above the minimum needed to keep it in its current use. The factor could be labour or another productive resource. In a labour example, the minimum is the reward needed to prevent the worker moving away from the specified use given the relevant alternative. The excess above that minimum is rent in the economic sense. It does not mean the worker makes no productive contribution or that receiving it is unlawful.

For a designer paid N$8,400 monthly who would remain for at least N$6,900, economic rent is N$1,500. The subtraction compares the actual reward with the minimum stated in the case. A housing payment described as rent in everyday speech is not automatically the same concept. Nor is total salary economic rent merely because the worker enjoys the job. We need the minimum reward or relevant alternative to identify the split. If that information is absent, explain the relationship rather than manufacture a numerical minimum. This distinction also prevents treating rent as the amount received when leaving a job: it is the excess within the current factor reward.

The current-use reference prevents a second common mistake. A worker might need a different minimum to remain with a particular employer than to remain in an occupation generally. A case specifying one employer’s alternative should not silently be interpreted as the minimum for the whole industry. Use the scope stated in the prompt and carry it through the subtraction.

blocks.heading: Transfer earnings and the reference alternative
blocks.text:
Transfer earnings are the minimum reward needed to retain a factor in its current use. They reflect the opportunity to put that factor to another use. The word transfer does not mean a government benefit or an electronic movement of funds. It identifies the threshold below which the factor would move away from the specified use. The relevant comparison could change if new alternatives appear, training improves access or conditions change. State the scope of the current use and the alternative rather than assuming one minimum applies permanently.

Using the designer example, N$6,900 is transfer earnings and N$1,500 is economic rent, together making N$8,400. If an improved alternative raises the minimum required to N$7,500 while current reward stays N$8,400, transfer earnings rise and rent falls to N$900. The actual total is unchanged. If the reward exactly equals the minimum, the example has no economic rent above that minimum. These calculations do not establish how much pay an employer can cut in practice; agreements, information and worker responses matter. They explain an economic decomposition relative to stated alternatives. This links to the comparison of earnings and to occupational choice (4.1): feasible alternatives help determine the minimum needed to retain a worker, while the actual reward can exceed it. Checking the split provides a useful arithmetic control: minimum plus excess must equal actual reward. If a proposed rent exceeds the whole reward despite a positive retention minimum, the labels or subtraction are wrong. The check validates the numerical decomposition, while identifying the relevant minimum remains an economic interpretation of the stated alternative.

blocks.heading: How earnings are determined
blocks.text:
Earnings are monetary rewards from work over a stated period. They can depend on the pay rate, hours worked, overtime, bonuses or other payment arrangements. A worker receiving more per month may simply work more paid hours. Compare like with like before explaining a difference. State whether figures are hourly, weekly or monthly and whether they include additional payments. An explanation of a wage rate is not automatically an explanation of total annual earnings.

Labour demand is related to the work employers need done and the value of the output workers help produce. Rising orders for an equipment-maintenance service can increase demand for its technicians. If trained applicants are scarce, employers may offer higher pay to recruit or retain them. Supply matters alongside demand: lengthy training or qualifications can limit the number able to enter quickly. Bargaining and employment arrangements, such as trade-union negotiation and a legal minimum wage, can also affect settlements. These influences interact, so a single label such as skilled does not prove a particular wage. Explain the demand for the skill, its availability and the relevant conditions. Dangerous or inconvenient work may require higher rewards to attract applicants, but workers’ alternatives and bargaining position affect whether such compensation is achieved.

Consider two reasons an employer might offer a higher wage. It may need more labour because customer orders increased, shifting demand for the work. Alternatively, fewer suitable applicants may be available because training places were limited. Both can put upward pressure on pay, but the initial changes differ. Distinguishing them helps explain why a later training expansion could ease recruitment pressure even if orders stay strong. The effect still depends on the amount of labour demanded and how workers respond to the offered terms.

Gross pay is total earnings before deductions. Net (take-home) pay is gross pay minus deductions such as income tax (PAYE), social security contributions, and pension and medical-aid contributions. Workers may be paid a time rate (a fixed amount per hour, week or month, as a wage or salary), a piece rate (a fixed amount for each unit produced), commission (a percentage of the value of sales), overtime (a higher rate for extra hours) or bonuses. Fringe benefits such as housing, transport or medical aid are non-wage rewards.

blocks.heading: The labour market on a diagram
blocks.text:
Draw the wage rate on the vertical axis and the quantity of labour on the horizontal axis. Labour demand slopes downwards, labour supply upwards, and the equilibrium wage is where they cross. In a coastal town, guest houses want 150 housekeepers at N$25 an hour and 150 will work for that wage. More tourists then raise the demand for rooms and so for housekeepers, because labour demand is derived demand: guest houses want 100 more at every wage. Labour demand shifts right, from D1 to D2; supply does not move. The wage rises to N$30 and employment to 200.

![Housekeeper labour market](diagrams/item-6145-4.2-025-proc-answer.png)

More trained workers would instead shift supply right and lower the wage. Strong trade unions (topic 2.2) may push wages above equilibrium, and a legal minimum wage (topic 6.3) sets a floor.

blocks.heading: Comparing different groups
blocks.text:
An earnings differential is a difference in rewards between workers or groups, measured on a comparable basis. Differences can arise from skills, experience, responsibilities, hours, employment continuity, location, bargaining and access to opportunities. Discrimination can also affect pay or entry to work. A descriptive average tells us that measured earnings differ; it does not identify how much each factor caused. To investigate, compare the jobs, hours and worker characteristics relevant to the question rather than assuming that the group label itself supplies an explanation.

For example, two employee groups average N$6,000 and N$7,500 a month. The raw difference is N$1,500. If one group works longer hours or contains more supervisors, that affects interpretation. The difference does not show that each worker in the higher-average group earns more than each worker in the other. Nor does it prove the gap is entirely explained by hours or that unfair treatment is absent. Better evidence is needed to separate these possibilities.

A common comparison basis is essential even for simple arithmetic. A difference between an hourly rate and a monthly total is not an earnings gap that can be meaningfully subtracted. If both figures are monthly, ask whether the months involve comparable hours and whether one includes a bonus. A summary may be useful for describing a workforce while remaining insufficient for judging equal work. The purpose of collecting more detail is to identify which comparison the evidence can support, rather than to dismiss a measured difference merely because several explanations are possible.

Typical reasons for differences in earnings are as follows. Skilled workers usually earn more than unskilled workers because training is long and costly, so supply is limited, while their higher productivity raises employers’ demand; unskilled labour is plentiful. On average men have earned more than women because women are more often in lower-paid occupations, more often take career breaks for childcare or work part-time, and may face discrimination in pay or promotion. Public-sector pay is set on national salary scales negotiated with government, often with more job security and pension benefits; private-sector pay depends more on profitability, performance and demand, so specialists may earn more there. Agricultural workers usually earn less than manufacturing and service workers because farm work is often seasonal, output per worker and its value are low, many workers are unskilled and few belong to trade unions. Services range from low-paid work (cleaning, retail) to very high-paid work (medicine, finance). Over time, earnings in an occupation rise relative to others when demand for it grows faster than supply (for example technology raising demand for IT technicians), when unions bargain successfully or when minimum wages or public salary scales are raised. They fall relatively when technology replaces the work or training expands supply.

blocks.heading: Changes over time and purchasing power
blocks.text:
Nominal earnings are rewards measured in current money without adjustment for prices. A rise in nominal pay does not establish an equal rise in purchasing power. Real income is income adjusted for the price level. If an illustrative salary rises from N$5,000 to N$5,500 while the relevant price index rises from 100 to 110, real salary at base-period prices is N$5,500 divided by 110 times 100, or N$5,000. The 10 percent nominal rise just matches the index change in this example. For exact comparisons use the index ratio rather than subtracting percentage rates and treating the approximation as exact.

Disposable income is a different concept: income available for spending and saving after relevant taxes and deductions. Removing a tax deduction does not adjust for prices. A worker can have higher disposable money income yet lower purchasing power if prices rise sufficiently. Keep the two adjustments separate. Use the deductions supplied in an exercise.

Relative earnings can also change across occupations or sectors. Technology may increase demand for some skills while reducing demand for tasks it replaces. Training can expand labour supply over time, and changes in product demand can alter employers’ need for workers. A growing occupation’s average might rise partly because it recruits more experienced staff. Compare consistent measures and avoid attributing a time change to one cause without evidence. An index converts money into a common purchasing-power basis; it does not identify the goods each household buys. Interpret the result for the stated basket and comparison period, and avoid inventing individual spending patterns.

blocks.heading: Splitting a factor reward
blocks.text:
A factor’s total reward can be divided into transfer earnings and economic rent. Transfer earnings are the minimum needed to retain the factor in its current use. Economic rent is the amount above that minimum. The split depends on the relevant alternative, so the reference use must be clear. It is not a division between wages and profit, and transfer earnings are not money transferred to a bank account.

Suppose a technician receives N$9,000 monthly and would remain in the current use for a minimum of N$7,200 given the stated alternative. Transfer earnings are N$7,200 and economic rent N$1,800. They sum to the actual reward of N$9,000. If the alternative changes so the minimum required becomes N$8,000 while actual pay stays fixed, rent falls to N$1,000. No cut in current pay is needed for the split to change. This connects earnings analysis to opportunity cost in topic 1.1: the minimum depends on what must be offered to retain the resource relative to its alternatives. It also links to occupational choice in 4.1 and bargaining in 2.2. Reward levels and the minimum needed to retain a factor answer different questions.

blocks.heading: Public operations and scarce resources
blocks.text:
The public sector comprises activities owned or controlled by government. Government can act as a producer of goods and services and as an employer of labour. These roles are connected but not identical. Producing output means combining resources to provide something useful; employing people means directly hiring them to perform work. Public employees can provide the labour needed for a service, while buildings, equipment and organisation also matter. A government paying an independent contractor for a task does not thereby directly employ the contractor’s whole workforce.

A publicly operated community facility may hire staff to maintain grounds and provide an information service. The facility provides output and employs workers. Its contribution should be assessed through the useful service and resources used, rather than merely the number hired. A service offered without a user fee still requires labour, equipment or other scarce inputs. Its opportunity cost is the alternative use of those resources. Funding it collectively changes how payment is arranged, rather than making production costless.

A public good is a specific economic category: non-rival and non-excludable. One person’s use does not reduce availability to others, and excluding non-payers is difficult. Not every government-provided service has these properties. A crowded classroom or an individual treatment can use scarce capacity. Nor does zero price make a service a free good; a free good has no opportunity cost in the relevant circumstances. This distinction links to scarcity in 1.1, government policy in 6.2 and the reasons for government intervention in 6.3. Classify by rivalry, exclusion and resource cost rather than by who pays or owns the provider alone. The funding arrangement and the economic properties of the output answer different questions and should be explained separately.

blocks.heading: Government as producer
blocks.text:
Government acts as producer when public operations combine resources to provide goods or services. The output may serve access, safety or other social objectives that are not captured by sales receipts alone. Producing a service still means using productive inputs: staff, equipment, premises and management must be available and organised. A financial loss does not by itself show a socially valuable service should cease, but a social aim does not remove the need to examine cost and effectiveness.

Consider a public information centre serving a remote community. It provides assistance that residents might otherwise have difficulty obtaining. The benefit concerns the actual service and access, not the centre’s government label. If funding is limited, spending on the centre has an opportunity cost in other possible services. Evaluate whether the output meets the intended need and whether its resources are used well. Paying no fee at the counter does not make staff time or equipment abundant. It also does not prove the output is a public good: access and capacity characteristics must be considered separately.

Provision, funding and production can differ. Government may fund a service produced by an independent supplier, or produce it through its own operations. Read the case before assigning the producer role. A public purchase shows demand for an output, whereas direct public production means the government operation itself combines the relevant inputs. This distinction makes later policy analysis clearer by identifying which activity and responsibility the evidence actually describes.

Government produces goods and services for several reasons. Public goods, such as national defence, street lighting and police protection, would be under-provided by private firms because non-payers cannot be excluded. Merit goods, such as education and health care, are goods whose benefits to the person and to society are greater than people realise, so they would be under-consumed if left to the market; government provides them free or at a low price. Government may also run essential services, such as electricity, water, rail transport and postal services, through state-owned enterprises (parastatals). It does this to make sure the services reach every region, including areas a private firm would find unprofitable, to stop a private monopoly exploiting consumers, or to keep control of strategic industries.

Privatisation is the transfer of a state-owned enterprise, or one of its activities, to private ownership. Arguments for privatisation: the profit motive may improve efficiency, the sale raises revenue for government, competition may lower prices and improve quality, and taxpayers no longer cover losses. Arguments against: a private owner may cut unprofitable services to remote areas, a private monopoly may raise prices, workers may be made redundant, and government loses control of strategic services. Nationalisation is the reverse: the state takes an industry into public ownership. Government may subsidise a loss-making state enterprise so that it keeps an essential service or jobs, but the subsidy has an opportunity cost in other spending.

blocks.heading: Government as employer
blocks.text:
Government acts as employer when it directly hires people for paid work in public operations. The employees provide labour services and receive remuneration under the relevant arrangements. Public work can involve many occupations, including administration, maintenance and specialised services. The ownership sector does not determine whether the job is manual, professional or clerical; those are separate occupational classifications.

Hiring staff can expand the ability to deliver a useful service when the right skills, equipment and organisation are available. If a public facility hires technicians but has no working equipment, employment numbers alone do not establish greater service output. Training, support and effective scheduling can affect how much satisfactory work is completed. Equally, an employee’s contribution cannot be judged from a government label without examining the task and resources. The economic comparison concerns the service benefit and the scarce resources needed.

A contractor’s staff and a public employee have different direct employers even when both work towards the same public project. This matters when describing the government as an employer rather than a purchaser. It also connects to earnings comparisons in 4.2: varied roles and conditions need a fair basis before comparing public and private rewards. Government employment can provide household income and support public output, while budget commitments and opportunity costs remain. A supported judgement identifies what work is needed and whether the arrangement delivers it effectively, rather than assuming either that public jobs are inherently unproductive or that more jobs necessarily mean a better service. A useful comparison also specifies the period. Hiring today can require induction before additional service is available, while an existing tool shortage may need attention sooner. Timing affects the feasible contribution of each option. Evidence should guide timing.

Government is one of the largest employers in the economy, employing teachers, nurses, police officers, soldiers, administrators and workers in state-owned enterprises. As an employer it provides public services, creates jobs in regions where private firms are few, and can reduce the number of people without work. The wages it pays become household income that is spent on goods and services, which raises demand, encourages firms to produce more and can contribute to economic growth. However, a large public wage bill must be financed by taxes or borrowing, and the money has an opportunity cost in other spending.

blocks.heading: Ownership and the activity performed
blocks.text:
The private sector comprises activity owned or controlled by private individuals or organisations. The public sector comprises activity owned or controlled by government. These terms classify ownership or control, not the stage of production. The sectors also differ in aim, finance and control. Private-sector firms usually aim to make a profit; public-sector organisations aim to provide services for the welfare of the public, such as water, electricity, education and health. Private firms are financed by owners’ capital, shares, loans and retained profit; public-sector organisations are financed mainly by government through taxes and borrowing, plus charges to users. Private firms are controlled by their owners or a board of directors; public-sector bodies are controlled by government, usually through a minister and an appointed board. A privately owned mine operates in the private sector and carries out primary activity. A state-owned manufacturer operates in the public sector and carries out secondary activity. A business providing services can likewise have private or public ownership. The words public company require particular care: shares being available to the public does not itself mean that government owns the business. Identify the owners or controlling organisation from the case. Do not infer ownership simply from the business being large, providing an important service or using the word public in a legal-form description.

Businesses can also be formal or informal. Formal businesses are registered, pay taxes and follow labour and licensing rules. Informal businesses, such as many street vendors and home-based traders, are not registered, usually operate on a small scale with little capital, and do not normally pay business taxes or keep formal records.

blocks.heading: The dimensions that distinguish forms
blocks.text: Compare business forms through several separate questions. Who owns the business and supplies its finance? Who controls daily decisions? Does the business have legal identity separate from its owners? What exposure do owners have to its debts? Can ownership interests be transferred, and what happens if an owner leaves? These dimensions can vary independently. A business may retain concentrated control while using an incorporated form, or have many shareholders who elect directors rather than manage daily work themselves. Limited liability concerns owners' legal exposure under the relevant rules; it does not mean that the business has no debts or that a creditor cannot lose money. A personal guarantee or a separate personal obligation can also matter.

blocks.heading: A form should match the decision
blocks.text: A repair business has one owner, modest equipment needs and customers who value the owner's personal work. Direct control and simplicity may favour sole ownership at that stage. If the owner wants a colleague's expertise and resources, joint ownership may become attractive, but the partners need an agreement about decisions and returns. If the activity requires larger commitments and a distinct legal entity, incorporation may be worth considering. The argument should use the needs in the case rather than assume that growth makes a particular form automatically best. Compare the finance obtained with the control shared, obligations accepted and risk exposure changed. A change of legal form does not by itself create customer demand or ensure that the business will earn enough to meet its commitments.

blocks.heading: Finance, control and risk can conflict
blocks.text: A wider group of owners may contribute more resources, while the original founder may prefer to retain decisions. Investors may expect information or influence in return for their funds. Formal governance and reporting can support accountability but use time and money. A suitable judgement identifies the strongest objective and the constraint that matters most. If the business cannot finance the necessary equipment from its present resources, retaining complete control may come at the cost of an expansion it cannot undertake. Alternatively, expansion may be unnecessary for a small service meeting its owners' goals. Weigh feasible alternatives and distinguish an owner benefit from a benefit to customers or workers. A recommendation must remain conditional on the actual finance, risk and management circumstances.

blocks.heading: Co-operation, state ownership and international scale
blocks.text: Not every organisation has the same purpose as a founder seeking personal profit. Members may establish a co-operative to purchase inputs or market output together. A public corporation may provide a service or pursue a strategic objective. Both still require resources and workable management. Multinational, meanwhile, identifies operations in more than one country rather than a separate universal legal form. A firm can operate across countries and also be described by its share-ownership arrangements. Exporting a product to another country does not by itself establish that the firm has productive operations there. Ask which feature the classification is describing. Keeping purpose, ownership, legal form and geographical operations separate makes comparisons more precise and avoids treating one label as a complete account of how the organisation works.

blocks.heading: A disciplined comparison
blocks.text: For a new case, identify the present arrangement, the proposed alternative and the business problem being addressed. Compare the forms using that problem rather than producing an unrelated list. Distinguish ownership from control and separate the business's obligations from owners' personal positions. Topic 2.3 develops financial institutions and raising funds, while topic 5.4 develops growth and integration. This topic concerns how ownership and organisation can serve the needs of the venture and its stakeholders. The most defensible conclusion explains why the selected form fits those needs and what change would make another option preferable. Control therefore concerns who makes decisions, while liability concerns whose assets may be used to meet debts.

blocks.heading: Sole proprietorship
blocks.text:
A sole proprietor is an individual owning an unincorporated business and bearing its obligations personally. The business may employ workers; sole ownership does not mean that the owner works alone. An alterations service owned by one person can employ an assistant while remaining a sole proprietorship. The owner can make decisions directly and receives the residual return after costs, but also bears the consequences if the venture performs poorly. Distinguish sales receipts from what remains for the owner after expenses. A sole proprietor has unlimited liability: if the business cannot pay its debts, the owner’s personal possessions, such as a house or car, can be used to pay them. This differs from a separate incorporated entity. The nature of the activity and the obligations undertaken affect the practical risk, so a simple ownership structure should not be described as risk-free merely because its initial costs are low.

Advantages of a sole proprietorship: it is easy and cheap to set up, decisions are quick, the owner keeps all the profit, the owner has close contact with customers, and the accounts can be kept private. Disadvantages: unlimited liability, limited capital (mainly the owner’s savings and loans), long working hours, and lack of continuity because the business may close if the owner dies or falls ill.

blocks.heading: When one owner may suit the activity
blocks.text: Sole ownership can suit a small activity where the owner's skill, customer relationships and desire for control are central. Decisions can be quick because agreement with other owners is not needed. However, finance may be limited by the owner's resources and ability to obtain it. The business can also depend heavily on that person's availability and expertise. If the owner becomes unavailable, providing the same service may be difficult. Additional workers can reduce some operational dependence without changing ownership. A judgement should compare these features with the activity's needs. An owner seeking a manageable personal service may value direct control more than large-scale expansion, while one facing a major investment requirement may prefer a form that brings other contributions. The preferred form is therefore connected to objectives rather than size alone.

blocks.heading: Partnership
blocks.text:
A partnership is a business owned by two or more partners (usually no more than 20), who share the capital, decisions and profits, normally under a written partnership agreement (deed). Partners can combine funds, knowledge, contacts and labour to operate the venture. Their agreement should address contributions, returns, decision-making and changes in participation. A design practice may bring together one partner with technical expertise and another with customer-management skills. The gain arises from complementary contributions rather than simply from adding names to the business. Do not assume that every partner contributes equal amounts or performs the same work unless the case says so. Legal responsibility depends on the partnership arrangement and applicable rules; a basic partnership should not be described as automatically providing the separate identity and limited liability of a company. Ordinary partners have unlimited liability, and the partnership may end when a partner dies or leaves.

Advantages of a partnership: more capital than one owner can supply, shared skills, workload and losses, and partners can cover for one another. Disadvantages: unlimited liability for ordinary partners, disagreements between partners, profits must be shared, each partner can be bound by the decisions of the others, and lack of continuity.

blocks.heading: Shared resources require workable agreement
blocks.text: Partnership can spread responsibilities and provide a wider resource base than one person could supply. A colleague's relevant skill can improve a weak part of the operation, while sharing tasks may help the business continue when one partner is absent. These benefits depend on cooperation. Disagreement about spending, workload or the use of profit can slow decisions and damage relationships. A clear agreement helps but cannot remove every possibility of conflict. Compare the resources obtained with the control shared and obligations accepted. If a repairer needs a partner's specialised skill, a partnership argument should explain that connection. Saying that partnership is better because there are more people omits both the quality of their contributions and the difficulty of coordinating them. An exit or dispute arrangement also matters when judging continuity.

blocks.heading: Private company
blocks.text: A private company is incorporated and has restricted share ownership rather than inviting unrestricted public subscription. Its separate legal identity distinguishes its rights and obligations from those of shareholders. Shares represent ownership interests, while directors manage the company within the relevant governance arrangements. A founder can remain closely involved in management, so incorporation does not automatically require distant or anonymous ownership. The restriction on public share availability distinguishes the private-company form from a public company; private here does not mean that the company must keep every activity secret. Official registration and ongoing obligations apply. A private company’s name ends with (Pty) Ltd. Its shares cannot be offered to the general public and are subject to transfer restrictions in the company’s articles. Advantages: limited liability, more capital than a partnership, continuity if a shareholder leaves, and the founders can keep control. Disadvantages: legal registration costs and formalities, capital is limited because shares cannot be sold to the public, and shares are not easy to sell.
blocks.repair_note: Codex cross-check of Claude additions: qualify company rules, monetary homogeneity and current payments, profit maximum, valuation and dependency conditions; preserve coverage additions.

blocks.heading: Separate identity and limited liability
blocks.text: Separate legal identity allows the company to hold rights and incur obligations as an entity distinct from its shareholders. Limited liability generally restricts shareholders' exposure for company debts to the obligations associated with their investment, subject to applicable rules and any separate commitments. It does not prevent a shareholder losing the money invested. Nor does it ensure that the company can pay its creditors. An owner who makes a separate personal guarantee may have an additional obligation. In an equipment business, incorporation may therefore matter to how obligations are organised, while lenders still assess the company's ability to repay. Compare legal exposure with commercial performance rather than claiming that the form supplies an automatic financial return. Reporting and administration can also impose costs that need to be considered against the benefits of incorporation.

blocks.heading: Public company
blocks.text:
A public company can offer shares to the public, subject to the applicable rules. This can widen access to equity finance compared with relying on a small invited ownership group. Shareholders own the company and receive part of the profit as dividends. They elect a board of directors, which controls and manages the company on their behalf. Wider share availability does not identify the government as owner. A public company can be part of the private sector. Nor does the word public alone establish that the company's shares are currently listed on a particular exchange. Distinguish the legal ability to offer shares from the separate arrangements for trading them. A manufacturer planning a substantial expansion might consider a wider ownership base, but the prospect of raising funds depends on investors' willingness to invest and the information available to them.

A public company’s name ends with Ltd, and its shares can be sold to the public, often through the Namibian Stock Exchange (NSX). Advantages: limited liability attracts investors, very large amounts of capital can be raised, shares are easy to transfer, and the company continues when shareholders change. Disadvantages: it is expensive and complex to set up, accounts must be published, ownership is separated from control, and there is a risk of takeover because anyone can buy shares.

blocks.heading: Ownership, control and wider finance
blocks.text: Wider share ownership can provide resources for an activity and make it easier for some owners to transfer their interests. It can also separate ownership from daily control because a large group of shareholders cannot each run the business. Directors then make decisions on the company's behalf and shareholders need suitable accountability arrangements. Additional reporting and governance can be costly but can provide information to investors. The original owners may have to share influence, and a change in the ownership pattern can affect control. When evaluating a public-company option, compare the capital requirement with the reporting burden and the owners' priorities. Do not assume that investors will buy shares merely because they are offered. The quality of the venture, expected return and perceived risk affect the finance actually obtainable.

blocks.heading: Multinational company
blocks.text: A multinational company has productive operations in more than one country. The label describes geographical operations rather than a universal legal form. A company can be a multinational and also have particular private or public share arrangements. A food processor with factories in two countries illustrates cross-border production. Selling exports from a single domestic factory, by contrast, does not by itself establish productive operations abroad. A business may expand internationally to reach customers, obtain inputs or organise stages of production in different locations. Those motives need to be connected to its activity. Different markets, transport arrangements, workforce capabilities and production conditions can influence the decision. International scale does not make the business immune to cost problems or prove that it benefits every country where it operates.

blocks.heading: Cross-border benefits and trade-offs
blocks.text: A host economy may gain employment, training, purchases from local suppliers or access to production knowledge from an international business. The size of those gains depends on how the operation uses local resources and the terms on which it operates. Some returns may leave the host economy, and local firms may face stronger competition. Decisions taken elsewhere may also affect local employment. For the company, operating in several countries can widen markets but creates coordination, information and management challenges. A comparison should identify whose interests are being considered: the owners, workers, customers or the host community. Avoid concluding that foreign operations are necessarily harmful or beneficial from the label alone. Use the actual activity, local links and alternative opportunities to judge the likely effects, and keep geographical scale separate from legal ownership classification.

blocks.heading: Co-operative
blocks.text: A co-operative is owned by members to pursue common economic interests through joint activity. Producers may cooperate to buy inputs, share facilities or market output, while consumers may organise to obtain goods or services for members. A group of growers could jointly use a packing facility that each would struggle to finance alone. Members' interests and participation are central to the purpose, rather than an assumption that one outside owner seeks the residual profit. Membership is voluntary, and each member usually has one vote whatever the size of the contribution (democratic control). Profits (surpluses) are shared among members, usually according to how much each bought from or supplied to the co-operative. Common types are producer co-operatives (for example farmers marketing crops together), consumer or retail co-operatives, and savings and credit co-operatives. For an economic comparison, explain how ownership by members connects to the shared service. A co-operative still needs resources, effective decisions and enough receipts or contributions to cover its activity. Mutual purpose does not remove scarcity or the need for financial discipline.

blocks.heading: Joint activity can help and constrain members
blocks.text: Combining members' purchases can improve their ability to obtain inputs, while shared equipment may spread costs over a larger volume of activity. Joint marketing can also make it easier to meet an order that would be too large for one member. These benefits depend on reliable contributions and suitable management. Members may disagree about prices, investment or the distribution of benefits, and reaching collective decisions can take time. Raising additional finance can also be difficult if available contributions are limited. A growers' co-operative should therefore be evaluated through its members' needs, the shared facility's use and the arrangements for paying and managing it. A useful judgement recognises the value of cooperation while asking whether the organisation can maintain quality, timely supply and fair participation under the stated constraints.

blocks.heading: Close corporation
blocks.text: In Namibia, a close corporation is a legal entity separate from its members and generally provides limited liability under the applicable law. Membership ownership distinguishes it from a sole proprietor's unincorporated activity. The entity's legal position also means that its obligations should not simply be treated as the personal obligations of its members because they belong to it. The protection is subject to the law and does not remove separate personal commitments or consequences of conduct for which members can be liable. A close corporation (CC) is registered under the Close Corporations Act with a founding statement. It has between one and ten members, who are normally natural persons (individuals), subject to the Act’s limited representative exceptions, and its name ends with CC. It suits small businesses that want limited liability without the formalities of a company. A small maintenance business may consider the form because the owners want to organise the venture separately from their personal affairs.
blocks.repair_note: Codex cross-check of Claude additions: qualify company rules, monetary homogeneity and current payments, profit maximum, valuation and dependency conditions; preserve coverage additions.

blocks.heading: A form is not a substitute for sound operation
blocks.text: A close corporation can be attractive where a small ownership group wants a distinct legal entity, but the business still needs customers, finance and workable management. Incorporation brings obligations rather than making administration disappear. Limited liability concerns how legal exposure is organised; the members can still lose invested resources if the venture performs poorly. A lender may also require information or additional security. Compare the form with the owners' objectives and circumstances rather than treating it as an automatic next step for every sole proprietor. If an existing business changes form, consider whether the change addresses a real need, such as organising several owners' participation or separating the entity's affairs.

blocks.heading: Public corporation
blocks.text: A public corporation is owned or controlled by the state and established for public purposes. Its objectives may include supplying an essential service, extending access or carrying out a strategic activity. It can charge for output and employ productive resources, so public purpose does not imply that its activity is costless. Distinguish the public corporation from a public company whose shares are available to private investors. The ownership and purpose need to be identified from the case. In an example, a state-controlled regional transport organisation may be required to maintain routes that are important for access but would not cover their costs at affordable fares. The arrangement can make wider objectives explicit, while creating a need to decide how the required resources are financed and accounted for.

blocks.heading: Public purpose and accountability
blocks.text: A public corporation can coordinate a service across areas or pursue an access goal not fully reflected in paying demand. However, its resources have alternative uses, and weak cost control or poor service can impose a burden on users and public finances. Clear objectives, reliable information and accountability matter. A judgement should compare performance against the stated purpose, not assume that profit is the sole criterion or that losses prove the service has no benefit. Equally, a public objective does not justify avoidable waste. For a transport service, examine the access gained, cost of delivery, feasible alternatives and quality achieved. Topic 6.1 develops government as producer and employer. The ownership form identifies who controls the organisation; explaining whether it serves its purpose requires evidence about what it actually does.

blocks.heading: Development and different starting conditions
blocks.text:
Economic development means improvement in economic and social conditions, including productive capacity, access to services and living conditions. It is broader than a larger output total. Developed and developing are broad descriptions of conditions, not a rule that residents share one income or that countries follow an identical path. Comparisons should identify evidence about productivity, income, education, health, infrastructure and opportunities rather than infer people’s abilities or preferences from a national label.

Capital resources, skills, institutions, geography, access to markets and historical conditions can influence development. Reliable transport can make trade and service access easier; suitable education can improve productive skills when opportunities exist. Limited finance or infrastructure can constrain investment, while weak coordination can reduce the benefit of available resources. These mechanisms interact and require evidence. A country rich in a particular resource does not automatically provide high living standards for each resident, since management, distribution and wider costs matter. When comparing Namibia with another country, use the relevant period, definition and indicators. A national average does not describe every household. A useful comparison asks what constrains a particular activity. Missing transport may raise market-access costs, while unavailable skills may limit use of equipment. Different constraints require different responses, and a single broad development label does not identify them. Evidence about services and opportunities also helps distinguish real improvements from a larger nominal income total caused by prices.

Developing economies usually have low real GDP per head, a large share of workers in the primary sector (farming, fishing, mining), high birth rates and often high death rates, a young population with a high dependency ratio, lower literacy and life expectancy, and weaker infrastructure. Developed economies usually have high real GDP per head, most workers in the tertiary (services) sector, low birth and death rates, an older population, high literacy and life expectancy, and good infrastructure. As a country develops, the share of output and employment in the primary sector tends to fall, the secondary (manufacturing) sector grows, and later the tertiary sector becomes the largest. Reasons for different stages of development include differences in capital, education and skills, infrastructure, natural resources, political stability, access to markets and rates of population growth.

blocks.heading: Adjustment as development proceeds
blocks.text:
Development can provide employment, infrastructure and access to goods and services, while changing how and where people live and work. Urbanisation is an increasing proportion of the population living in urban areas. It can bring people closer to employers, education and services, but requires housing, transport, water and other capacity. If settlement grows faster than infrastructure, congestion or poor access can offset some benefits. The process is not automatically either a problem or a success; compare the resources and opportunities available.

An expanding town gains processing and repair work. Workers and firms may benefit from proximity and shared services, while authorities face pressure to plan transport and housing. Some existing activities may contract or need new skills. Gains can be distributed unevenly, so a higher town output does not prove each family benefits. Environmental effects and the opportunity cost of infrastructure should also be considered. A supported explanation identifies the initial economic change, the adjustment it requires and the possible consequence for a specified group. Policy needs to fit those constraints instead of simply urging everyone to move. Development is a change in productive and living conditions, whose quality depends on access, distribution and sustainable use of resources. The pace of adjustment matters to both costs and gains. Infrastructure takes time to plan and provide, while household needs occur immediately. A short-term bottleneck can therefore coexist with a longer-term opportunity. State the time horizon and the affected groups rather than treat development as one instant change with equal effects everywhere.

Problems as a country develops include rapid rural-urban migration and the growth of informal settlements, a shortage of jobs when job creation lags behind the growing labour force, pollution and environmental damage from industry, depletion of natural resources, widening income inequality between regions and groups, loss of traditional skills and culture, and government borrowing for infrastructure that leads to debt. Developed countries face different problems, such as an ageing population, high pension and health-care costs, labour shortages and congestion.

blocks.heading: Population accounting and reasons for change
blocks.text:
Natural population change is births minus deaths in a period. Total change adds immigration and subtracts emigration. All components need the same geographical boundary and period. In a district with 10,000 initial residents, 250 births, 100 deaths, 200 arrivals and 150 departures, natural increase is 150 and net migration 50. Total increase is 200, giving 10,200 residents if no other statistical adjustments are assumed. The 200 arrivals alone are not net migration, and the 150 natural increase alone is not total change.

Birth rates tend to be high where children are seen as extra labour or support in old age, where family planning is less available or less used, where people marry young, and where cultural or religious values favour large families. Birth rates tend to fall as women’s education and employment increase and as the cost of raising children rises. Death rates fall with better health care, clean water, sanitation, nutrition and vaccination, and rise with disease such as HIV and AIDS or with famine. Net migration rises when a country offers more jobs, higher wages or greater safety than its neighbours. Population grows quickly when birth rates stay high while death rates fall. Age composition, education and household circumstances also matter. For Namibia or another country, distinguish a reasoned mechanism from a verified current trend. A population with many people entering reproductive ages can have substantial births even when a fertility measure falls. Changes in mortality can affect natural increase, while movement towards work or services can alter local populations. It is not enough to say a place develops and therefore its population must grow at one fixed rate. Interpret the specific components and circumstances. Births, deaths, fertility and migration are defined carefully so that a count, a per-thousand rate and a per-woman measure are not treated as interchangeable. A percentage rate should use the population basis requested. In the district illustration, 200 additional residents relative to the initial 10,000 gives 2 percent total growth. That is not the same measure as the birth rate alone or the net-migration count. Keep additions and rates separate, and do not add percentages with incompatible denominators as though they were counts.

blocks.heading: Size, structure and the economic response
blocks.text:
Population size is the total number, while structure describes its composition, including age. A larger child population can increase demand for schooling and family services. More older residents can change care, accessibility and income-support needs. A larger working-age group can increase potential labour supply and demand for products. The actual effect depends on health, skills, productive resources and opportunities, not simply a person crossing an age threshold.

Suppose a population is 1.8 million and 62 percent belongs to the age group specified in a task. The number is 0.62 times 1,800,000 =1,116,000 people, or 1.116 million. Labelling it 1,116 million would create a thousandfold error. An age-group percentage also does not tell us how many actually work or depend on others. Some working-age people are studying or lack jobs; some older people work. Ratios using age bands are indicators with assumptions rather than exact records of dependency.

A larger market can support firms and more specialisation, but it also requires housing, infrastructure and investment. If real output fails to keep pace, output per person can fall. A policy judgement should identify which needs and resources change, the response time and how gains or burdens are distributed. This links population to employment in 7.2, output in 7.3 and living standards in 8.2. Do not equate more people with economic growth or assume one age structure guarantees prosperity. Population structure can also change without a large total change. A place may have similar resident numbers but a larger older share, altering the type of service demand. Another may attract working-age arrivals and need housing near jobs. Planning therefore needs composition as well as size. The economic mechanism follows the specific needs and resources, not the total alone. Movement between regions redistributes service demand even when national population is unchanged. A supported response therefore connects the level of the decision—local or national—to the boundary of the demographic evidence and the resources that can actually be redirected.

The age-dependency ratio compares people in dependent age bands (often under 15 and 65 or over) with the working-age population (15–64): age-dependency ratio = (population in the dependent age bands ÷ working-age population) × 100. A high ratio means more people in those age bands per 100 working-age people, which can put pressure on education, health and pensions. It does not count actual dependants per employed worker: some working-age people do not work and some older people do. An ageing population raises spending on pensions and health care and can cause labour shortages. Rapid population growth can strain government aims: more people may be without work if jobs grow more slowly than the labour force, GDP per head falls if output grows more slowly than population, housing, schools, clinics, water and food come under pressure, and resources are used up faster. This is why a government may try to slow high population growth through education, family-planning services and incentives.

blocks.heading: Birth rate and birth numbers
blocks.text:
The crude birth rate is live births during a year per thousand people in the relevant population. Calculate births divided by population, multiplied by 1,000, using a consistent population basis when the exercise supplies it. In an area with 300 births and 20,000 people, the rate is 15 births per thousand. It is neither 15 percent nor 300 births per thousand. Units and denominator distinguish the rate from the number of births.

The same rate can produce different counts. At 15 per thousand, 40,000 people correspond to 600 births in the simplified calculation. Comparing 300 births in one place with 600 in another therefore does not establish a higher birth rate without population information. Age structure also matters because the crude rate uses the entire population as denominator rather than only people in reproductive ages. A change in the number and age distribution of potential parents can affect total births separately from individual childbearing patterns. This helps explain why births need not fall immediately when a fertility measure declines. For a supplied Namibia or international comparison, read the year, population and measure rather than inventing a current trend. The calculation gives a defined summary, while explaining the summary needs relevant demographic and economic evidence. Births contribute to natural change, but deaths and migration are still needed for a complete population-accounting conclusion. If a problem supplies a population in millions, convert consistently before obtaining a count. A rate per thousand multiplied by a population count must also be divided by a thousand. Writing both steps protects against a large scale error. The rate’s meaning is unchanged by the display unit, while the arithmetic must use compatible numbers.
